chaos.name: Chaos
chaos.desc:
The first of all things, Chaos is the primordial void — a yawning, formless gap that existed before anything else. From this emptiness the earliest beings arose of their own accord: Gaia the earth, Tartarus the abyss, Erebus the darkness, and Nyx the night.

Chaos is less a deity with a story than the raw, gaping origin out of which the ordered cosmos slowly took shape.

gaia.name: Gaia
gaia.desc:
The primordial Earth, Gaia arose from the first yawning Chaos as the deep-rooted foundation of all things, and from herself brought forth Uranus the sky, the mountains and the barren sea. Mother and grandmother of gods, Titans, Giants and monsters, she is the elemental source of every generation — yet also its great avenger, arming Cronus against Uranus and later loosing Typhon and the Giants against Zeus.

Her oracles spoke at Delphi long before Apollo claimed them.

uranus.name: Uranus
uranus.desc:
The primordial sky, Uranus was born of Gaia and became her mate, fathering the twelve Titans, the Cyclopes and the hundred-handed Hecatoncheires. A tyrant, he loathed his monstrous children and crushed them back into the earth, until Gaia armed their son Cronus, who castrated him and flung the severed parts into the sea — from the foam rose Aphrodite, and from the fallen blood the avenging Furies.

His overthrow began the succession of divine kings.

nyx.name: Nyx
nyx.desc:
The primordial Night, Nyx is among the very first beings to emerge from Chaos — a goddess so ancient and formidable that even Zeus holds her in awe. Robed in dark mist, she draws night over the world and brings forth, often without a father, a brood of powerful abstractions: Death and Sleep, the Fates, Doom, Strife, Nemesis and deceitful Dreams.

She dwells at the edge of the cosmos and rises each evening as her daughter Day withdraws.

erebus.name: Erebus
erebus.desc:
A primordial god of darkness, Erebus emerged from Chaos among the very first beings — the deep shadow that fills the hollow spaces of the underworld through which the dead must pass.

With his sister Nyx the Night he fathered Aether, the bright upper air, and Hemera, the Day, so that from the deepest darkness light itself was born.

tartarus.name: Tartarus
tartarus.desc:
Both a primordial god and the deep abyss that bears his name, Tartarus is the pit that lies as far below Hades as the earth lies below the sky. Born of Chaos, he became the dungeon of the cosmos — the prison into which Zeus hurled the defeated Titans, sealed behind bronze gates and guarded by the hundred-handed giants.

With Gaia he fathered the monstrous Typhon, the last great challenger to Olympus.

pontus.name: Pontus
pontus.desc:
The primordial sea, Pontus was brought forth by Gaia the Earth without a father — the first salt water and the deep from which the older sea-gods descend.

With his own mother he fathered a line of ancient marine deities: Nereus the truthful old man of the sea, monstrous Ceto, Phorcys, Thaumas and Eurybia — the ancestors of nymphs, gorgons and sea-monsters alike.

cronus.name: Cronus
cronus.desc:
Youngest and boldest of the Titans, Cronus overthrew his father Uranus at Gaia's urging — castrating the sky-god with an adamant sickle — and ruled the cosmos through a golden age. Warned by prophecy that his own child would unseat him in turn, he swallowed each of his offspring at birth, until Rhea hid the infant Zeus and fed him a stone in swaddling clothes.

Grown, Zeus forced him to disgorge his siblings and cast him down in the ten-year Titanomachy, ending the reign of the Titans.

rhea.name: Rhea
rhea.desc:
A Titaness of the earth and motherhood, Rhea was sister and wife to Cronus and mother of the first Olympians. When her husband devoured each child at birth to cheat prophecy, she saved her youngest by giving Cronus a swaddled stone to swallow and spiriting the infant Zeus away to Crete, where nymphs and the clashing Curetes drowned out his cries.

Through that single act of a grieving mother, the entire Olympian order came to be.

oceanus.name: Oceanus
oceanus.desc:
Eldest of the Titans, Oceanus is the vast fresh-water river believed to encircle the flat disc of the world, the source of every sea, spring and stream. With his sister-wife Tethys he fathered the three thousand river-gods and the three thousand Oceanid nymphs.

Aloof from the strife of the gods, he took no part in the Titanomachy and kept to his ancient realm at the rim of the earth, a figure of primeval, untroubled power.

tethys.name: Tethys
tethys.desc:
A Titaness of fresh water and nurse of the sea, Tethys is the mother of all the world's rivers and springs. With her brother-husband Oceanus, the encircling stream, she bore the three thousand river-gods and the three thousand Oceanid nymphs — the source of every flowing water on earth.

Ancient and untroubled, she took no part in the Titanomachy and remained a gentle, generative power at the world's rim.

hyperion.name: Hyperion
hyperion.desc:
A Titan of heavenly light, Hyperion is the lord of watchfulness whose name means the one who goes before. With his sister Theia he fathered the three great lights of the sky — Helios the sun, Selene the moon, and Eos the dawn — so that through him the ordered movement of day and night came into being.

He fought with his brother Titans against the Olympians and shared in their fall into Tartarus.

theia.name: Theia
theia.desc:
A Titaness of light and the shining sky, Theia is the goddess through whom gold, silver and gems were thought to gleam, the source of the heavens' brightness.

With her brother Hyperion she bore the luminaries — Helios, Selene and Eos — and so is mother of the sun, the moon and the dawn, the very lights by which the world is seen.

themis.name: Themis
themis.desc:
A Titaness of divine law, order and prophecy, Themis embodies the natural and moral order of the cosmos — the customs by which gods and mortals rightly live. An early holder of the Delphic oracle, she became a trusted counsellor of Zeus, seated beside his throne, and bore him the Horae (the Seasons) and the Moirae (the Fates).

She is justice personified, even-handed and older than the Olympian order she helps uphold.

mnemosyne.name: Mnemosyne
mnemosyne.desc:
The Titaness of memory, Mnemosyne holds the recollection of all things — vital in an age before writing, when knowledge lived only in the mind. Lying with Zeus for nine nights, she bore the nine Muses, goddesses of poetry, music and the arts, so that through memory came the power to preserve and celebrate the deeds of gods and heroes.

The dead were said to drink from her pool to remember their past lives.

iapetus.name: Iapetus
iapetus.desc:
A Titan bound up with mortal life and its darker fate, Iapetus fathered — by the Oceanid Clymene — Atlas, Prometheus, Epimetheus and Menoetius. Through these sons he stands as ancestor of the failings of humankind: Prometheus its cunning, Epimetheus its heedless folly, Atlas its endurance under punishment.

He fought against the Olympians in the Titanomachy and was hurled down with his brothers into Tartarus.

coeus.name: Coeus
coeus.desc:
A Titan of the heavenly axis and of far-seeing intelligence, Coeus is linked to the pillar of the north around which the stars forever wheel. With his sister Phoebe he fathered Leto and Asteria, and so is grandfather to Apollo and Artemis.

He rose with his brothers against the Olympians and was cast down with them into the pit of Tartarus.

phoebe.name: Phoebe
phoebe.desc:
A Titaness of bright prophecy, Phoebe was an early mistress of the oracle at Delphi, which she passed in time to her grandson Apollo. With her brother Coeus she bore Leto and Asteria, making her grandmother to the twin archer-gods.

Her name, meaning radiant, marks her as a goddess of the shining, prophetic power of the moonlit heavens.

leto.name: Leto
leto.desc:
A gentle Titaness of motherhood, Leto was loved by Zeus and so became a special target of Hera's jealousy. Hunted across the world and refused shelter by every land that feared the queen's wrath, she found refuge at last on the barren floating island of Delos, where she gave birth to the twin archer-gods Apollo and Artemis.

From that hard labour came two of the mightiest Olympians, and Leto ever after guarded her children's honour without mercy.

metis.name: Metis
metis.desc:
A Titaness of wisdom and deep cunning, Metis was the first great counsellor of Zeus and, in some tellings, his first wife — it was her draught that forced Cronus to disgorge the swallowed Olympians. But warned that Metis would bear a child mightier than its father, Zeus swallowed her whole while she was pregnant, taking her wisdom into himself.

From his own head then sprang their daughter Athena, fully armed, while Metis lived on as the shrewd inner voice of the king of the gods.

atlas.name: Atlas
atlas.desc:
A Titan of endurance and the heavens, Atlas led the Titans in their war on the Olympians and, for his part, was condemned by Zeus to bear the weight of the sky upon his shoulders at the western edge of the world.

Brother of Prometheus and father of the Pleiades and the nymphs of the Hesperides, he was briefly relieved of his burden by Heracles, and in one tale was turned to the stone of the Atlas Mountains by the severed head of Medusa.

prometheus.name: Prometheus
prometheus.desc:
The Titan of forethought and cunning, Prometheus sided with Zeus in the Titanomachy but became mankind's great champion against the gods. He shaped humanity from clay, tricked Zeus over the division of sacrifice, and stole fire from Olympus in a fennel stalk to give it to mortals.

For this Zeus chained him to a Caucasian crag where an eagle tore at his ever-renewing liver each day, until Heracles at last freed him — the enduring image of defiant sacrifice.

zeus.name: Zeus
zeus.desc:
King of the gods and lord of the sky, Zeus overthrew his father Cronus, won the heavens as his portion, and rules Olympus with the thunderbolt forged for him by the Cyclopes. Youngest child of Cronus and Rhea, he was hidden away on Crete to escape his son-devouring father, then freed his swallowed siblings and led them to victory in the ten-year Titanomachy.

Guardian of oaths, hospitality and kingship, he upholds cosmic order — yet his endless disguised affairs, and Hera's jealous revenge on his lovers and their children, set half the myths of gods and mortals in motion.

hera.name: Hera
hera.desc:
Queen of the gods and goddess of marriage, Hera is both sister and wife to Zeus, presiding over women, wedlock and the household. Regal and unforgiving, she wages relentless vengeance on her husband's countless lovers and their offspring — hounding Heracles from the cradle, tormenting Io and Leto, and nursing the grudges that ripple through the Trojan cycle.

Her jealousy is not mere spite but the wounded pride of a betrayed queen, and few myths of Zeus unfold without her shadow falling across them.

poseidon.name: Poseidon
poseidon.desc:
Lord of the sea, earthquakes and horses, Poseidon drew the ocean as his realm when the three brothers divided the cosmos after the fall of the Titans. Wielding the trident forged by the Cyclopes, he raises storms and shatters coastlines when angered, and his long feud with Odysseus keeps that hero wandering for ten bitter years.

Fiercely proud, he lost his contest with Athena for Athens when her olive tree outshone his salt spring, and fathered a brood of giants and monsters — the man-eating Cyclops Polyphemus among them.

hades.name: Hades
hades.desc:
Grim lord of the dead, Hades rules the shadowed underworld that bears his name, the third portion drawn by the sons of Cronus. Aloof from Olympus, he seldom leaves his kingdom, keeping the souls of the departed with the help of the hound Cerberus and a helm that renders its wearer invisible.

His one great myth is the abduction of Persephone, whom he carried below to be his queen — a bargain that binds her to him for a third of every year and gives the mortal world its winter.

demeter.name: Demeter
demeter.desc:
Goddess of grain, harvest and the fruitful earth, Demeter feeds gods and mortals alike and holds the secret of the seasons. When Hades stole her daughter Persephone into the underworld, her grief withered every field until the world began to starve, forcing Zeus to broker the girl's partial return — her joy the summer, her mourning the barren winter.

From that sorrow and reunion grew the Eleusinian Mysteries, the most revered of Greek initiations, which promised their initiates a blessed life beyond death.

hestia.name: Hestia
hestia.desc:
The gentle goddess of the hearth, home and sacred flame, Hestia was the eldest child of Cronus and Rhea — first swallowed and last disgorged, and so both oldest and youngest of the Olympians. Preferring peace to the quarrels of the gods, she gave up her Olympian throne to Dionysus and took as her portion the ever-burning hearth-fire at the heart of every home and city.

A sworn virgin honoured with the first offering of every sacrifice, she is the quiet, steady centre of both household and state.

athena.name: Athena
athena.desc:
Goddess of wisdom, craft and strategic war, Athena sprang fully grown and armoured from the head of Zeus, after he swallowed her pregnant mother Metis. Patron of heroes and of the city that bears her name — won from Poseidon by her gift of the olive tree — she favours cunning over brute force, steadying Odysseus, Perseus and Heracles through their trials.

A sworn virgin, aegis-bearing and grey-eyed, she embodies the disciplined intelligence the Greeks prized above raw strength, and turned the boastful weaver Arachne into a spider for daring to rival her.

apollo.name: Apollo
apollo.desc:
God of light, prophecy, music, healing and plague, Apollo is the radiant son of Zeus and Leto and twin of Artemis, born on the floating island of Delos. Master of the lyre and the silver bow, he speaks the will of Zeus through his oracle at Delphi, which he won by slaying the earth-serpent Python.

Beautiful yet often unlucky in love — Daphne fled him into laurel, Hyacinthus died by his own discus — he is a god of both the sudden gift and the sudden arrow, bringing harmony or pestilence as he chooses.

artemis.name: Artemis
artemis.desc:
Goddess of the hunt, wild beasts, the moon and young girls, Artemis is the twin of Apollo and a fiercely sworn virgin who roams the mountains with her band of nymphs. Armed with a silver bow, she is swift to punish any who violate her chastity or her woods — she turned the hunter Actaeon into a stag to be torn apart by his own hounds for glimpsing her at her bath.

Protector of the young and of women in childbirth, she is at once nurturing and utterly merciless.

ares.name: Ares
ares.desc:
God of war in its brutal, bloody aspect, Ares embodies the frenzy and slaughter of the battlefield, set against Athena's cool strategy. A son of Zeus and Hera disliked by both his parents, he is more feared than loved, and myth often shows him bested — wounded by the mortal Diomedes at Troy, snared in a net by Hephaestus while dallying with Aphrodite.

From that affair came Harmonia and the terror-twins Phobos and Deimos, Fear and Dread, who ride at his side into the carnage he relishes.

hephaestus.name: Hephaestus
hephaestus.desc:
God of fire, the forge and craftsmanship, Hephaestus is the divine smith whose skill shapes the wonders of Olympus — Zeus's thunderbolts, Achilles' armour, and the first woman Pandora. Cast down from heaven and left lame, he is the only Olympian marked by ugliness and hard toil, yet his artistry has no equal.

Married to unfaithful Aphrodite, he trapped her and Ares in an unbreakable net and summoned the gods to mock them. Patient and ingenious, he answers every slight with cunning craft rather than force.

hermes.name: Hermes
hermes.desc:
God of travellers, thieves, merchants, heralds and boundaries, Hermes is the quick-witted messenger of the gods and the guide who leads souls down to Hades. Son of Zeus and the nymph Maia, he was a trickster from his first day — stealing Apollo's cattle and inventing the lyre from a tortoise shell to buy his pardon.

Winged of sandal and cap, he moves freely between the worlds of the living, the dead and the divine, carrying messages, striking bargains, and lending his cunning to heroes like Odysseus and Perseus.

aphrodite.name: Aphrodite
aphrodite.desc:
Goddess of love, beauty and desire, Aphrodite rose from the sea-foam where the severed heavens fell — older, in that telling, than the Olympians she joins. Irresistible and capricious, she stirs longing in gods and mortals alike, and it was her promise of Helen to Paris that lit the Trojan War.

Wedded to the smith Hephaestus but bound to Ares, she meddles endlessly in the loves of others — blessing devoted Pygmalion, and cursing those who scorn her rites or dare to boast themselves more fair.

dionysus.name: Dionysus
dionysus.desc:
God of wine, ecstasy, theatre and ritual madness, Dionysus is the twice-born son of Zeus and the mortal Semele, snatched from her ashes and sewn into his father's thigh to be carried to term. He wanders the world with a wild train of maenads and satyrs, bringing the gift of the vine and the liberating frenzy of his rites — and terrible ruin to proud kings like Pentheus who deny his godhood.

God of the mask and the dissolving of boundaries, he offers both joyous release and savage retribution.

persephone.name: Persephone
persephone.desc:
Goddess of spring's growth and dread queen of the underworld, Persephone is the daughter of Zeus and Demeter, seized by Hades as she gathered flowers and carried below to rule the dead at his side. Because she tasted the seeds of a pomegranate there, she is bound to the underworld for a portion of each year; her descent is the world's winter, her return its spring.

Maiden and queen at once, she embodies the yearly death and rebirth of the earth, gentle above and terrible below.

maia.name: Maia
maia.desc:
The eldest and shyest of the seven Pleiades, Maia was a mountain nymph who dwelt alone in a cave on Mount Cyllene. There she was loved by Zeus and bore him the god Hermes — whom she raised in secret, only for the precocious infant to slip from his cradle on his very first day to steal the cattle of Apollo.

She was set with her sisters among the stars as the Pleiades.

semele.name: Semele
semele.desc:
A princess of Thebes and mother of the god Dionysus, Semele was a mortal woman loved by Zeus. Tricked by the jealous Hera into demanding that her divine lover reveal himself in his true form, she was consumed by the blaze of his glory — but Zeus snatched the unborn Dionysus from her ashes and sewed him into his own thigh to be born.

She was later raised from the dead to dwell among the gods.

helios.name: Helios
helios.desc:
The Titan of the sun, Helios drives his blazing four-horse chariot across the sky each day from his eastern palace to the western sea, seeing and hearing all that passes below. It was he who told grieving Demeter of Persephone's fate and who exposed the affair of Ares and Aphrodite.

His reckless son Phaethon begged to drive the sun-chariot, lost control and scorched the earth until Zeus struck him down; and the sacred cattle of Helios, slaughtered by Odysseus's starving crew, doomed them all.

odysseus.name: Odysseus
odysseus.desc:
The cleverest of the Greek heroes, Odysseus, king of Ithaca, was famed for cunning and endurance above raw strength — it was his stratagem of the Wooden Horse that finally took Troy after ten years of siege.

But his boast and the blinding of the Cyclops Polyphemus earned the wrath of Poseidon, condemning him to ten more years of wandering: past Circe and the Sirens, between Scylla and Charybdis, held captive by Calypso — before he came home at last, disguised and alone, to reclaim his wife Penelope and his throne from a house full of suitors.

penelope.name: Penelope
penelope.desc:
The faithful wife of Odysseus and queen of Ithaca, Penelope waited twenty years for her husband's return, matching his cunning with her own. Besieged by more than a hundred suitors who devoured her household and pressed her to remarry, she held them off with a famous ruse — weaving a burial shroud by day and unravelling it each night, vowing to choose only when it was done.

Her patience is the still centre of the Odyssey, rewarded when Odysseus returned in disguise, slaughtered the suitors, and proved himself to her by the secret of their marriage bed.

telemachus.name: Telemachus
telemachus.desc:
The only son of Odysseus and Penelope, Telemachus was still an infant when his father sailed for Troy, and grew to manhood in a house overrun by his mother's suitors. Stirred by the goddess Athena, he set out on his own journey to seek news of his father, coming of age in the search.

When Odysseus returned at last in disguise, father and son were reunited and together slaughtered the suitors to reclaim their home.

laertes.name: Laertes
laertes.desc:
The aged father of Odysseus and former king of Ithaca, Laertes had withdrawn to his farm in grief and old age during his son's twenty-year absence, wearing himself out with toil and sorrow.

When Odysseus finally returned and revealed himself, the old man was restored to vigour by Athena and took up arms one last time, fighting at his son's side against the vengeful kin of the slain suitors.

nestor.name: Nestor
nestor.desc:
The aged king of Pylos and wisest of the Greek leaders at Troy, Nestor was famed for his long experience and his gift for counsel, having outlived three generations of men. Too old to match the young warriors in battle, he served instead as the elder statesman of the Greek camp, offering advice and telling tales of the heroes of his own youth.

He survived the war and returned safely to his kingdom to reign in honoured old age.

menelaus.name: Menelaus
menelaus.desc:
King of Sparta and husband of Helen, Menelaus was the wronged party whose stolen wife launched the Trojan War. Brother of the high commander Agamemnon, he fought bravely at Troy and faced Paris in single combat, nearly killing him before Aphrodite spirited the prince away.

After the city's fall he reclaimed Helen and, following long wanderings of his own, returned with her to Sparta to reign again.

helen.name: Helen
helen.desc:
The most beautiful woman in the world, Helen was a daughter of Zeus born to Leda of Sparta, and wife to King Menelaus. When Paris carried her off to Troy — whether seduced or seized — every Greek king who had once sworn to defend her marriage was bound to sail against the city, launching the thousand ships of the Trojan War.

Blamed and pitied in equal measure, she watched the ten-year slaughter fought over her from the walls of Troy, and in the end returned to Sparta and Menelaus.

eumaeus.name: Eumaeus
eumaeus.desc:
The loyal swineherd of Odysseus, Eumaeus kept faith with his absent master through all his long years away, tending the herds and offering hospitality to strangers.

When Odysseus returned disguised as a beggar, it was in Eumaeus's humble hut that he first found shelter, and the faithful servant fought at his side in the slaughter of the suitors — a model of humble loyalty rewarded.

antinous.name: Antinous
antinous.desc:
The most arrogant and aggressive of Penelope's suitors, Antinous led the crowd of young nobles who feasted on Odysseus's household and plotted to murder his son Telemachus.

Cruel and insolent even to the disguised Odysseus, whom he struck as a mere beggar, he was the first to fall when the hero at last revealed himself — an arrow through his throat as he raised a cup to drink.

nausicaa.name: Nausicaa
nausicaa.desc:
A young princess of the Phaeacians, Nausicaa found the shipwrecked Odysseus washed naked and exhausted upon her shore while she played with her maids. Unafraid, she gave him clothing and food and guided him to her father's palace, where he won the help that would finally carry him home.

Gracious and kind-hearted, she is one of the gentlest figures of the Odyssey.

alcinous.name: Alcinous
alcinous.desc:
The generous king of the Phaeacians, Alcinous ruled a blessed seafaring people on a far and prosperous island.

He welcomed the shipwrecked Odysseus into his palace, listened spellbound to the long tale of his wanderings, and loaded him with gifts before providing the magical ship that at last bore the hero home to Ithaca as he slept.

tiresias.name: Tiresias
tiresias.desc:
The great blind prophet of Thebes, Tiresias was the most famous seer of Greek myth, who had lived as both man and woman and understood the speech of birds. Blinded by a goddess but granted prophecy in recompense, he foretold the doom of Oedipus and the fall of Thebes.

Even in death his wisdom endured — his was the shade Odysseus sought in the underworld to learn the way home.

circe.name: Circe
circe.desc:
A goddess-witch and daughter of the sun-god Helios, Circe dwelt on the island of Aeaea, mistress of potions and transformations. When Odysseus's men landed there she turned them into swine with a touch of her wand — until Odysseus, shielded by a herb from Hermes, overcame her magic and won her as his host and lover for a year.

Far from an enemy, she became his guide, restoring his men and telling him how to pass the Sirens, brave Scylla and Charybdis, and reach the land of the dead.

calypso.name: Calypso
calypso.desc:
A beautiful nymph and daughter of the Titan Atlas, Calypso lived alone on the hidden island of Ogygia, where the shipwrecked Odysseus washed ashore. She kept him with her for seven years, offering him immortality and eternal youth if he would only stay as her husband — yet he pined always for home and his wife Penelope.

At last Zeus sent Hermes to command his release, and Calypso, grieving, helped him build a raft and sent him off with wind and provisions.

polyphemus.name: Polyphemus
polyphemus.desc:
A one-eyed Cyclops and son of Poseidon, Polyphemus was a giant herdsman who lived in a cave on his island, caring nothing for gods or the laws of hospitality. When Odysseus and his men sheltered there, he trapped them and devoured them two at a time — until Odysseus made him drunk, put out his single eye with a burning stake, and escaped clinging beneath his sheep.

But by boasting his true name as he sailed away, Odysseus let the blinded giant call down his father Poseidon's curse of long wandering.

scylla.name: Scylla
scylla.desc:
A six-headed sea-monster, Scylla was once a beautiful nymph, transformed by a jealous rival into a horror with twelve groping feet and six long necks, each ending in a head with triple rows of teeth. She lurked in a cliffside cave above a narrow strait, snatching sailors from passing ships.

Odysseus lost six of his men to her jaws as he was forced to steer close beneath her to avoid the deadly whirlpool Charybdis opposite.

charybdis.name: Charybdis
charybdis.desc:
A vast sea-monster in the form of a churning whirlpool, Charybdis lurked beneath a narrow strait directly opposite the cave of Scylla. Three times a day she swallowed down the sea and belched it back, destroying any ship caught in her maw.

Sailors passing through were forced into a deadly choice — steer close to Scylla and lose a few men, or risk Charybdis and lose all — the origin of being caught between two evils.

sirens.name: Sirens
sirens.desc:
Enchantresses of the sea, the Sirens were part-woman, part-bird creatures whose irresistible song lured passing sailors onto their rocks, to perish among the bones of earlier victims. Warned by Circe, Odysseus alone contrived to hear their song and live — stopping his crew's ears with wax and having himself lashed to the mast, straining against his bonds as they rowed safely past.

It was said the Sirens would die if any mortal heard their song and escaped, and so at his passing they flung themselves into the waves.

thetis.name: Thetis
thetis.desc:
A sea-nymph of great beauty and one of the fifty Nereids, Thetis was courted by Zeus himself — until a prophecy warned that her son would be greater than his father, and the gods married her to a mortal instead. From that union came Achilles, whom she sought to make immortal by dipping him in the Styx, and whom she armed and counselled through the war, knowing all the while she was fated to outlive him.

Her grief for her doomed son runs like a thread through the Iliad.

achilles.name: Achilles
achilles.desc:
The greatest warrior of the Greeks at Troy, Achilles was son of the sea-nymph Thetis and the mortal Peleus, dipped as a baby in the river Styx so that only the heel she held remained vulnerable. Half-divine, swift and terrible, he knowingly chose a short life of undying glory over a long and quiet one.

His wrath at Agamemnon — who seized his war-prize Briseis — withdrew him from battle at ruinous cost, until the death of his beloved Patroclus drove him back to slay Hector, before he himself fell to an arrow guided to his heel.

agamemnon.name: Agamemnon
agamemnon.desc:
King of Mycenae and commander of all the Greek forces at Troy, Agamemnon was the brother of Menelaus and the mightiest lord of his age. To win fair winds for the fleet he sacrificed his own daughter Iphigenia — a crime that would damn him — and his proud quarrel with Achilles over the captive Briseis nearly cost the Greeks the war.

He took Troy at last, but returning home in triumph was murdered in his bath by his wife Clytemnestra and her lover, avenging their daughter's death.

ajax.name: Ajax
ajax.desc:
The mighty bulwark of the Greeks, Ajax the Great was the tallest and strongest of the warriors at Troy, second in prowess only to Achilles. Wielding a huge tower-like shield, he held the line against Hector and duelled him to a standstill, and it was he who carried the dead Achilles from the field.

But when Achilles' divine armour was awarded to Odysseus instead of him, his wounded pride drove him mad, and in shame he fell upon his own sword.

diomedes.name: Diomedes
diomedes.desc:
One of the bravest and most level-headed of the Greek captains at Troy, Diomedes was a favourite of Athena, who lent him such fury that he wounded even the gods — driving his spear into Ares and Aphrodite themselves upon the field. Wise as well as bold, he joined Odysseus in the daring night-raid on the Trojan camp and the theft of the sacred Palladium.

Alone among the great Greek leaders, he came home from the war unscathed.

patroclus.name: Patroclus
patroclus.desc:
The dearest companion of Achilles, Patroclus was raised beside him in the house of Peleus and followed him to Troy as his closest friend and, in many tellings, his lover. Gentle and beloved throughout the Greek camp, it was he who — seeing his countrymen driven back to their ships — borrowed Achilles' own armour and led the Myrmidons out to turn the tide.

He drove the Trojans to their walls before Hector cut him down, and his death shattered Achilles, drawing the great warrior back into a war he had forsworn.

briseis.name: Briseis
briseis.desc:
A princess taken captive when Achilles sacked her city, Briseis became his prize of honour and, in the poems, his beloved. When Agamemnon seized her from him to salve his own wounded pride, the insult drove Achilles into the furious withdrawal from battle that shapes the whole of the Iliad.

Her loss and later return move through the epic as the human stake behind the wrath of Achilles.

hector.name: Hector
hector.desc:
The noblest of the Trojans and their greatest defender, Hector was the eldest son of King Priam and heir to Troy. A devoted husband to Andromache and father to the infant Astyanax, he fought not for glory but for his city and family, killing many Greeks and leading the assault that reached their very ships.

When he slew Patroclus he sealed his own doom: Achilles hunted him down beneath the walls, killed him in single combat, and dragged his body behind his chariot — until Priam came alone in the night to beg his son back for burial.

priam.name: Priam
priam.desc:
The aged king of Troy through the years of the war, Priam was father to fifty sons — Hector and Paris among them — and watched his city besieged for ten long years. A figure of tragic dignity, his most moving hour comes when he steals alone into the Greek camp to beg Achilles for the body of his slain son Hector, moving even that furious hero to pity.

He lived to see Troy fall and was cut down at his own altar on the night the city burned.

paris.name: Paris
paris.desc:
A prince of Troy and the spark of its ruin, Paris was exposed at birth for a prophecy that he would destroy the city, but grew up a shepherd on Mount Ida. Chosen to judge the fairest of three goddesses, he awarded the golden apple to Aphrodite in return for the most beautiful woman alive — Helen, wife of Menelaus of Sparta.

Carrying her off to Troy, he lit the ten-year war; a handsome but reluctant fighter, he later killed Achilles with an arrow before falling himself.

andromache.name: Andromache
andromache.desc:
The devoted wife of Hector and a princess of Troy, Andromache is one of the great tragic figures of the Iliad, having already lost her father and brothers to Achilles. Her tender farewell to Hector at the city gates — their infant son Astyanax frightened by his father's plumed helmet — is among the poem's most human moments.

When Troy fell she lost husband and child both, and was carried off into slavery by the victorious Greeks.

heracles.name: Heracles
heracles.desc:
The greatest of all Greek heroes, Heracles was a son of Zeus by the mortal Alcmene, endowed with superhuman strength and hounded all his life by the jealousy of Hera. Driven mad by the goddess, he killed his own wife and children, and in penance was bound to serve King Eurystheus, who set him the Twelve Labours — slaying the Nemean Lion and the Hydra, capturing Cerberus, cleansing the Augean stables and more.

Through these feats and many others he won at his death a place among the gods on Olympus, wedded to Hebe — the only mortal hero to become fully divine.

perseus.name: Perseus
perseus.desc:
A son of Zeus by the mortal Danae, Perseus was among the earliest and greatest of the Greek heroes, conceived when Zeus came to Danae as a shower of golden rain in her prison tower. Sent to fetch the head of the Gorgon Medusa, he was aided by Athena and Hermes with a mirrored shield, winged sandals and a cap of invisibility, and beheaded her by watching only her reflection.

Returning home, he used her petrifying head to rescue the princess Andromeda from a sea-monster and to turn his enemies to stone.

theseus.name: Theseus
theseus.desc:
The great hero and legendary king of Athens, Theseus was raised in secret and journeyed to claim his birthright, clearing the road of bandits and monsters along the way. His most famous deed was the slaying of the Minotaur in the Cretan Labyrinth, finding his way back out by the thread of the princess Ariadne, whom he then abandoned on Naxos.

As king he unified Attica under Athens, but his later adventures — carrying off Helen, descending into the underworld — ended in exile and a lonely death.

jason.name: Jason
jason.desc:
The leader of the Argonauts, Jason was rightful heir to the throne of Iolcus, sent by his usurping uncle to fetch the Golden Fleece in the hope he would never return. Gathering the greatest heroes of the age aboard the ship Argo, he sailed to distant Colchis and won the Fleece with the help of the sorceress-princess Medea, who fell in love with him and betrayed her own father.

But his later abandonment of Medea for another bride brought a terrible revenge upon his house, and he died alone and unremembered.

bellerophon.name: Bellerophon
bellerophon.desc:
A Corinthian hero and slayer of monsters, Bellerophon won and tamed the winged horse Pegasus with a golden bridle given him by Athena. Falsely accused and sent on a suicidal errand, he mounted Pegasus and killed the fire-breathing Chimera from the air.

Grown proud from his triumphs, he at last dared to fly up to Olympus itself to join the gods — but Zeus sent a gadfly to sting Pegasus, throwing him down to end his days lamed and broken.

orpheus.name: Orpheus
orpheus.desc:
The greatest musician of myth, Orpheus was son of the Muse Calliope, and his lyre could charm beasts, trees and even stones. When his wife Eurydice died of a snakebite, he descended alive into the underworld and so moved Hades and Persephone with his song that they released her — on the one condition that he not look back until they reached the light.

He looked, and lost her forever.

atalanta.name: Atalanta
atalanta.desc:
A fierce huntress and the swiftest of mortals, Atalanta was exposed at birth for being a girl and raised in the wild by a bear. She drew first blood in the great hunt for the Calydonian Boar and sailed, in some tellings, with the Argonauts.

Vowing to marry only a man who could outrun her — and to kill those who lost — she was beaten at last by a suitor who dropped three golden apples to slow her in the race.

daedalus.name: Daedalus
daedalus.desc:
The greatest craftsman and inventor of myth, Daedalus built the Labyrinth on Crete to hold the Minotaur, and gave Ariadne the thread by which Theseus escaped it.

Imprisoned by the angry King Minos, he fashioned wings of feathers and wax for himself and his son Icarus to fly to freedom — a masterwork of ingenuity shadowed by the tragedy that followed.

oedipus.name: Oedipus
oedipus.desc:
The tragic king of Thebes, Oedipus was fated by prophecy to kill his father and marry his mother, and was abandoned as an infant to escape it. Grown to manhood in ignorance of his birth, he unknowingly did both — slaying Laius at a crossroads and winning Jocasta and the throne by solving the riddle of the Sphinx.

When the truth came at last to light, Jocasta hanged herself and Oedipus put out his own eyes in horror.

cadmus.name: Cadmus
cadmus.desc:
The founder and first king of Thebes, Cadmus was a Phoenician prince sent to seek his abducted sister Europa. Guided by an oracle, he slew a great serpent sacred to Ares and, on Athena's advice, sowed its teeth in the earth — from which sprang armed warriors who fought until only five remained to help him raise the city.

He married Harmonia, though their line would be cursed by tragedy.

meleager.name: Meleager
meleager.desc:
A prince of Calydon and one of the heroes of the age, Meleager led the great hunt for the monstrous Calydonian Boar. His life was bound by fate to a burning log, which his mother had snatched from the fire and hidden at his birth.

When he killed his own uncles in a quarrel over the boar's hide, his grieving mother cast the log back into the flames — and as it burned away, so did his life.

castor.name: Castor
castor.desc:
One of the twin Dioscuri, Castor was the mortal brother of the immortal Pollux, sons of Leda — great horsemen, warriors and protectors of sailors both.

When Castor was slain in a cattle-raid, his devoted twin could not bear to be parted from him and shared his own immortality, so the brothers might remain together, set at last in the sky as the constellation Gemini.

pollux.name: Pollux
pollux.desc:
One of the twin Dioscuri, Pollux was the immortal son of Zeus and Leda, while his beloved twin Castor was mortal — great horsemen and protectors of sailors both. When Castor was slain, Pollux was so stricken with grief that he begged Zeus to let him share his own immortality with his brother.

Zeus granted it, setting the twins together in the sky as the constellation Gemini, dividing their days between Olympus and the underworld.

eros.name: Eros
eros.desc:
The primordial and Olympian god of love and desire, Eros is the force that draws all things together — in the oldest tellings born from Chaos at the dawn of creation, in later myth the mischievous winged son of Aphrodite. Armed with a bow whose golden arrows kindle irresistible love and whose leaden ones breed cold rejection, he strikes gods and mortals alike at his whim.

His own great love was for the mortal princess Psyche, whom he won at last after she endured the jealous trials set by his mother.

pan.name: Pan
pan.desc:
The god of the wild, of shepherds, flocks and mountain wilds, Pan is a rustic deity with the horns, legs and hooves of a goat. Playful and lustful, he roams the hills chasing nymphs and napping in the noonday heat — his sudden shout able to strike whole armies with mindless panic.

When the nymph Syrinx fled him and became a bed of reeds, he cut them into the pipes that bear her name and so became the maker of music.

iris.name: Iris
iris.desc:
The goddess of the rainbow and swift messenger of the gods, Iris links heaven and earth as her shimmering arc bridges sky and ground. A daughter of the sea-god Thaumas, she carries the commands of the Olympians — especially of Hera, whom she serves — travelling on golden wings to the depths of the sea and the underworld alike.

She fills the clouds with water for the rains and refreshes the gods from the streams of the world.

nike.name: Nike
nike.desc:
The winged goddess of victory, Nike presides over triumph in war and in every contest, swooping down to crown the victors of battle and games with glory. Daughter of the Titan Pallas and the river Styx, she and her siblings — Zelus (Rivalry), Kratos (Strength) and Bia (Force) — stood with Zeus in the war against the Titans and were made his constant companions ever after.

She flies at the side of the gods, bearing the wreath and palm of the champion.

hebe.name: Hebe
hebe.desc:
The goddess of youth, Hebe is the daughter of Zeus and Hera and the cupbearer of the gods, pouring the nectar and ambrosia that keep the Olympians forever young. Grace and blooming youthfulness personified, she served at the divine feasts until she was given in marriage to the deified Heracles as his reward for a life of labour — a union that crowned the hero's ascent to Olympus.

She had the power to restore the aged to the vigour of youth.

eris.name: Eris
eris.desc:
The goddess of strife and discord, Eris is the grim companion of war who delights in the quarrels of gods and men.

Snubbed from the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, she took her revenge by tossing among the goddesses a golden apple inscribed to the fairest — the seed of the rivalry and the Judgement of Paris that set the whole Trojan War in motion.

hecate.name: Hecate
hecate.desc:
A goddess of magic, witchcraft, the night, ghosts and crossroads, Hecate holds power across the sky, the earth and the underworld alike. Honoured even by Zeus, who left her ancient privileges untouched, she carries twin torches and roams the night with a pack of spectral hounds, haunting the places where three roads meet.

She alone helped Demeter search for the stolen Persephone, and became the maiden queen's companion below — a guide between the worlds of the living and the dead.

nemesis.name: Nemesis
nemesis.desc:
The goddess of divine retribution, Nemesis is the stern power who punishes hubris — the overweening pride and undeserved fortune that offend the gods — restoring the balance that fate demands. She metes out sorrow to the arrogant and the excessively lucky, ensuring none rise too high without a fall.

It was she, in one telling, who was pursued by Zeus and laid the egg from which Helen was born, and she who lured proud Narcissus to his end.

eos.name: Eos
eos.desc:
The rosy-fingered goddess of the dawn, Eos rises each morning from the eastern ocean to open the gates of heaven for her brother Helios the sun, scattering the dew and pushing back the night. Daughter of the Titans Hyperion and Theia, she was cursed by Aphrodite with an insatiable love for mortal men and carried off many handsome youths.

For her beloved Tithonus she begged Zeus for immortality but forgot to ask for eternal youth — so he withered endlessly, shrinking at last into a chirping cicada.

selene.name: Selene
selene.desc:
The goddess of the moon, Selene drives her silver chariot across the night sky, drawn by pale horses, as her brother Helios drives the sun by day.

Daughter of the Titans Hyperion and Theia, she is best known for her love of the beautiful shepherd Endymion, for whom she begged Zeus an eternal sleep so that he might never age or die — visiting him each night in his cave, where she bore him many daughters.

asclepius.name: Asclepius
asclepius.desc:
The god of medicine and healing, Asclepius was a son of Apollo, raised and taught the healing arts by the wise centaur Chiron until his skill surpassed that of all mortals. So great was his power that he could raise the very dead — until Zeus, fearing he would upset the order between mortals and gods, struck him down with a thunderbolt.

Honoured thereafter as a god, his temples became places of healing, and his serpent-entwined staff remains the emblem of medicine to this day.

hypnos.name: Hypnos
hypnos.desc:
The gentle god of sleep, Hypnos is a son of Night and the twin brother of Death, dwelling in a misty cave at the edge of the world through which the river of forgetfulness flows. Calm and kindly, he brings rest to weary gods and mortals alike, able to lull even Zeus into slumber — as Hera once persuaded him to do, at great risk, to work her will in the Trojan War.

From his cave stream the many Dreams, his children.

thanatos.name: Thanatos
thanatos.desc:
The god of death itself, Thanatos is a son of Night and twin of Sleep, the gentle-cruel bringer of a peaceful end who carries mortals down to the underworld when their time has come.

Even-handed and merciless, hated by gods and men for taking without regard to rank or worth, he was twice cheated — chained for a time by the crafty Sisyphus so that none could die, and later wrestled down by Heracles to win back Alcestis from the grave.

calliope.name: Calliope
calliope.desc:
The eldest and greatest of the nine Muses, Calliope is the Muse of epic poetry and eloquence, chief of her sisters and often shown with a writing tablet. She inspired the grandest of songs — the deeds of gods and heroes sung by Homer — and was accounted the wisest and most commanding of the Muses.

She was mother of the divine musician Orpheus, whose power to move stones and beasts with song was her gift to him.

moirai.name: The Fates
moirai.desc:
The three Fates, the Moirai are the ancient goddesses who spin, measure and cut the thread of every mortal life — Clotho who spins it, Lachesis who measures its length, and Atropos who severs it at death. Older and more inexorable than the gods themselves, their decrees even Zeus is loath to overturn.

Impartial and unmoved by prayer, they apportion to each soul its due of good and ill from birth to the appointed hour of death.

chiron.name: Chiron
chiron.desc:
The wisest and most just of the centaurs, Chiron was unlike his wild and violent kin — immortal, learned, and a great teacher of gods and heroes. A master of medicine, music, hunting and prophecy, he tutored many of the greatest, Achilles, Jason and Asclepius among them.

Accidentally struck by one of Heracles' poisoned arrows and unable to die, he suffered until he gave up his immortality to free Prometheus, and was set among the stars.

typhon.name: Typhon
typhon.desc:
The most monstrous of all creatures, Typhon was a colossal serpentine giant, born of Gaia and Tartarus, whose hundred dragon-heads brushed the stars and whose voices roared like beasts and gods alike. He rose to overthrow Zeus himself, and in their world-shaking battle briefly cut the very sinews from the king of the gods — until Zeus recovered, blasted him with a hundred thunderbolts, and buried him beneath Mount Etna, where he still spews fire.

By the she-viper Echidna he fathered many of the great monsters of myth.

echidna.name: Echidna
echidna.desc:
The mother of monsters, Echidna was a fearsome creature — half beautiful woman, half monstrous serpent — who dwelt in a cave and never aged nor died. Mate to the giant Typhon, she brought forth a horrifying brood that plagued the heroes of myth: Cerberus, the Hydra, the Chimera, the Sphinx, the Nemean Lion and more.

Through her, nearly every great monster of Greek legend shares a single dreadful lineage.

medusa.name: Medusa
medusa.desc:
The only mortal of the three monstrous Gorgon sisters, Medusa was once a beautiful maiden, transformed — in the best-known telling — into a snake-haired horror whose gaze turned any who met it to stone. She was slain by the hero Perseus, who approached using his polished shield as a mirror to avoid her petrifying stare and struck off her head.

From her severed neck sprang the winged horse Pegasus, and her head kept its stone-turning power, set at last upon the shield of Athena.

minotaur.name: Minotaur
minotaur.desc:
A monstrous creature with the body of a man and the head of a bull, the Minotaur was born to Pasiphae, queen of Crete, after she was cursed to love a bull. King Minos hid the beast at the heart of the Labyrinth, a maze from which none could escape, and fed it a tribute of Athenian youths and maidens.

It was slain at last by the hero Theseus, who found his way back out of the maze by following a thread given him by Minos's daughter Ariadne.

chimera.name: Chimera
chimera.desc:
A fire-breathing monster of Lycia, the Chimera was a grotesque hybrid — a lion at the fore, a goat rising from its back, and a serpent for a tail.

Offspring of Typhon and Echidna, it laid waste to the countryside with its flames until the hero Bellerophon, mounted on the winged horse Pegasus, attacked it from the air and drove a lead-tipped spear into its throat, where the creature's own fiery breath melted the metal and choked it.

hydra.name: Lernaean Hydra
hydra.desc:
A gigantic serpentine water-monster with many venomous heads, the Lernaean Hydra haunted the swamps of Lerna, its breath and blood so toxic that even its scent could kill. Its terror lay in regeneration — for every head struck off, two grew in its place.

Heracles overcame it as the second of his labours, his nephew Iolaus searing each stump with fire so no new head could sprout, and afterward he dipped his arrows in its poisonous blood.

cerberus.name: Cerberus
cerberus.desc:
The monstrous hound of the underworld, Cerberus is a three-headed dog with a serpent for a tail and snakes bristling along his back, who guards the gates of Hades. He lets the dead pass freely in but allows none to leave and no living soul to enter.

His capture — dragged up to the surface world bare-handed — was the twelfth and greatest of the labours set for Heracles, the one creature the hero could not simply kill.

sphinx.name: Sphinx
sphinx.desc:
A monster with the face of a woman, the body of a lion and the wings of an eagle, the Sphinx was sent to plague the city of Thebes.

She perched above the road and strangled all who could not answer her riddle: what walks on four legs at dawn, two at noon, and three at dusk? When Oedipus answered correctly — man — she flung herself to her death from the cliff in defeat.

nemean_lion.name: Nemean Lion
nemean_lion.desc:
A monstrous lion with a hide no weapon could pierce, the Nemean Lion terrorised the countryside around Nemea, devouring all who came near. Its slaying was the first of Heracles' twelve labours: unable to wound it with arrow or club, the hero cornered it in its cave and strangled it with his bare hands.

He then wore its impenetrable pelt as a cloak and its head as a helm ever after.

pegasus.name: Pegasus
pegasus.desc:
The immortal winged horse, Pegasus sprang from the blood of the Gorgon Medusa when Perseus struck off her head. A creature of radiant beauty, he was tamed by the hero Bellerophon with a golden bridle from Athena and carried him aloft to slay the Chimera.

When Bellerophon later tried to fly to Olympus, Pegasus threw him and flew on alone, to be kept by Zeus and set at last among the stars.

python.name: Python
python.desc:
A monstrous serpent-dragon, Python was the offspring of Gaia the Earth and the original guardian of the oracle at the centre of the world.

The young god Apollo slew it there with his arrows to claim the shrine for his own — founding his great oracle at Delphi over the creature's remains, and instituting the Pythian Games in memory of the deed.

ladon.name: Ladon
ladon.desc:
A hundred-headed dragon that never slept, Ladon was set to guard the tree of golden apples in the Garden of the Hesperides at the world's western edge. Coiled forever about the tree, he was overcome by Heracles in the course of his eleventh labour — slain, or lulled, so the hero could take the sacred fruit.

Hera set the faithful serpent among the stars as the constellation Draco.

cetus.name: Cetus
cetus.desc:
The great sea-monster sent by Poseidon to ravage the coast of Ethiopia, Cetus was the beast to which the princess Andromeda was chained as a sacrifice to appease the god.

As it rose from the deep to devour her, the hero Perseus swooped down and slew it — in some tellings turning it to stone with the severed head of Medusa — and claimed the freed princess as his bride.

harpies.name: Harpies
harpies.desc:
Winged spirits of the storm-wind, the Harpies were foul creatures with the faces of women and the bodies of birds, snatching people and things away in sudden gusts. Their most famous torment was of the blind seer Phineus, whose food they stole or fouled at every meal, until the winged sons of the North Wind drove them off.

Swift and filthy, they were the very spirit of the sudden, thieving squall.

argus.name: Argus Panoptes
argus.desc:
A giant with a hundred eyes covering his body, Argus Panoptes — the all-seeing — was the perfect watchman, for some of his many eyes always stayed awake while others slept. Hera set him to guard the heifer Io, Zeus's transformed lover, until Hermes lulled every eye to sleep with his music and slew him.

In his memory Hera set his hundred eyes upon the tail of her sacred peacock.

cyclopes.name: The Cyclopes
cyclopes.desc:
The elder Cyclopes were three one-eyed giants — Brontes, Steropes and Arges (Thunder, Lightning and Brightness) — sons of Uranus and Gaia and master smiths of the primordial world.

Imprisoned first by their father and then by the Titans, they were freed by Zeus in the war against the Titans, and in gratitude forged for him the mighty thunderbolts that won him the cosmos, along with Poseidon's trident and Hades' helm of darkness.

alcmene.name: Alcmene
alcmene.desc:
A mortal princess of great virtue and beauty, Alcmene was the mother of Heracles by Zeus, who came to her disguised as her own husband while the real one was away at war. So she bore twin sons on the same night — the divine Heracles to Zeus and the mortal Iphicles to her husband.

Her devotion and her famous son made her one of the most honoured of mortal women, revered even after her death.

danae.name: Danae
danae.desc:
A princess of Argos, Danae was shut away in a bronze chamber by her father Acrisius, who had been warned by prophecy that her son would one day kill him. But Zeus came to her as a shower of golden rain, and she bore the hero Perseus.

Cast adrift with her infant in a wooden chest, she was saved on a distant shore and later reunited with her grown son, whose stray discus would at last fulfil the old prophecy.

europa.name: Europa
europa.desc:
A Phoenician princess of great beauty, Europa caught the eye of Zeus, who took the form of a gentle white bull and mingled with her father's herds. When she climbed trustingly onto his back, he plunged into the sea and carried her across the waves to Crete.

There she bore him three sons — Minos, Rhadamanthys and Sarpedon — and gave her name to the continent of Europe.

io.name: Io
io.desc:
A priestess of Hera loved by Zeus, Io was turned into a white heifer — by Zeus to hide the affair, or by jealous Hera — and set under the guard of the hundred-eyed Argus. When Hermes slew the watchman, Hera sent a maddening gadfly that drove Io wandering across the world in torment, giving her name to the Ionian Sea and the ox-ford of the Bosphorus.

She found peace at last in Egypt, restored to human form.

leda.name: Leda
leda.desc:
A queen of Sparta, Leda was visited by Zeus in the form of a swan, and from that union — twined with her mortal husband's — she brought forth two famous eggs. From them hatched Helen, the most beautiful woman in the world, and Pollux, alongside Clytemnestra and Castor.

Through her children she stands at the root of both the Trojan War and the tragedy of the house of Atreus.

minos.name: Minos
minos.desc:
The powerful king of Crete and a son of Zeus and Europa, Minos ruled a great sea-empire and gave his name to the Minoan world. When he failed to sacrifice a magnificent bull sent by Poseidon, the god cursed his wife Pasiphae to bear the Minotaur, which Minos hid away in the Labyrinth built by Daedalus.

So just was his rule that after death he was made one of the three judges of the dead in the underworld.

pasiphae.name: Pasiphae
pasiphae.desc:
A queen of Crete and daughter of the sun-god Helios, Pasiphae was a sorceress in her own right and wife to King Minos. When Minos withheld a magnificent bull from sacrifice, Poseidon cursed her with an unnatural passion for the beast, and she had the craftsman Daedalus build a hollow wooden cow in which to approach it.

From that union she bore the Minotaur, the bull-headed monster hidden away in the Labyrinth.

ariadne.name: Ariadne
ariadne.desc:
A princess of Crete and daughter of King Minos, Ariadne fell in love with the hero Theseus when he came to face the Minotaur. She gave him the ball of thread by which he found his way back out of the Labyrinth, and fled with him — only to be abandoned on the island of Naxos.

There she was found and wed by the god Dionysus, who set her bridal crown among the stars.

phaedra.name: Phaedra
phaedra.desc:
A princess of Crete and younger sister of Ariadne, Phaedra became the wife of the hero Theseus.

Struck by a doomed and unlawful passion for her stepson Hippolytus, she was spurned by the chaste youth, and in shame and despair she took her own life — leaving behind a false accusation that drove Theseus to call down a fatal curse upon his innocent son.

aegeus.name: Aegeus
aegeus.desc:
A king of Athens and father of the hero Theseus, Aegeus sent his son to face the Minotaur in Crete, bidding him raise white sails on his return if he lived.

When the victorious Theseus forgot, and his ship approached under its black mourning-sails, Aegeus — believing his son dead — threw himself from the cliffs into the sea, which ever after bore his name: the Aegean.

icarus.name: Icarus
icarus.desc:
The son of the great craftsman Daedalus, Icarus escaped imprisonment on Crete with his father on wings of feathers and wax. Warned to fly neither too low, lest the sea's damp weigh the wings, nor too high, lest the sun melt them, the boy was seized by the sheer joy of flight and soared too near the sun.

The wax melted, his wings fell apart, and he plunged into the sea that bears his name.

medea.name: Medea
medea.desc:
A princess of Colchis and a powerful sorceress, granddaughter of the sun, Medea fell in love with Jason and used her magic to win him the Golden Fleece, betraying her father and killing her own brother to flee with him.

When Jason later abandoned her for another bride, her love turned to a terrible vengeance — she killed the new bride and then her own children by Jason, escaping in a chariot drawn by dragons.

aeetes.name: Aeetes
aeetes.desc:
The king of distant Colchis and keeper of the Golden Fleece, Aeetes was a son of the sun-god Helios and father of the sorceress Medea.

When Jason and the Argonauts came for the Fleece, he set them seemingly impossible tasks — yoking fire-breathing bulls and sowing a dragon's teeth — never dreaming his own daughter's magic would help the hero prevail and carry off both Fleece and princess.

pelias.name: Pelias
pelias.desc:
The usurping king of Iolcus, Pelias seized the throne that rightly belonged to his nephew Jason, and sent the young hero to fetch the Golden Fleece in the certain hope he would never return.

When Jason came back triumphant, the sorceress Medea contrived his downfall — persuading his own daughters to cut him up and boil him, on the false promise that it would restore his youth.

jocasta.name: Jocasta
jocasta.desc:
The queen of Thebes, Jocasta was wife first to King Laius and then, unknowingly, to her own son Oedipus. Having given up her infant son to die and so escape a dread prophecy, she later married the young stranger who had solved the Sphinx's riddle — never knowing he was that same son, returned.

When the incest was revealed, she hanged herself in despair.

laius.name: Laius
laius.desc:
The king of Thebes and father of Oedipus, Laius was warned by an oracle that his own son would kill him.

He gave the infant Oedipus to be exposed on a mountainside to prevent it — but the child survived, and years later Laius was killed in a roadside quarrel by a young stranger he did not know to be that same son, fulfilling the prophecy he had tried to escape.

antigone.name: Antigone
antigone.desc:
A princess of Thebes and daughter of Oedipus, Antigone is a figure of unbending moral courage. When her two brothers killed each other in civil war and King Creon forbade the burial of the one he named a traitor, she defied the edict to bury her brother, holding the law of the gods above the law of the state.

For this she was condemned to be sealed alive in a tomb, where she took her own life.

andromeda.name: Andromeda
andromeda.desc:
An Ethiopian princess, Andromeda was chained to a rock as a sacrifice to a sea-monster to atone for her mother Cassiopeia's boast of surpassing beauty. The hero Perseus, flying past on his return from slaying Medusa, saw her plight, slew the monster, and freed her — winning her as his bride.

She was set at last among the stars beside her rescuer.

cepheus.name: Cepheus
cepheus.desc:
The king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda, Cepheus was forced by his wife's boastful pride to chain his own daughter to a rock as a sacrifice to a sea-monster.

Spared that grief by the timely arrival of the hero Perseus, who slew the beast and wed the princess, he too was set among the stars as a constellation.

cassiopeia.name: Cassiopeia
cassiopeia.desc:
The vain queen of Ethiopia and mother of Andromeda, Cassiopeia boasted that her beauty surpassed that of the sea-nymphs themselves. For this hubris Poseidon sent a sea-monster to ravage her land, which could be appeased only by the sacrifice of her daughter.

Placed among the stars as a constellation, she was set to circle the pole forever, half the time hanging upside down in humiliation.

clytemnestra.name: Clytemnestra
clytemnestra.desc:
The queen of Mycenae and wife of Agamemnon, Clytemnestra never forgave her husband for sacrificing their daughter Iphigenia to gain fair winds for Troy.

While he was away at war she took his cousin Aegisthus as her lover, and on his triumphant return she murdered him in his bath — only to be killed in turn by her own son Orestes, avenging his father.

deianira.name: Deianira
deianira.desc:
The second wife of Heracles, Deianira became the unwitting instrument of his death. Given what she believed was a love-charm by the dying centaur Nessus — in truth a deadly poison — she smeared it on a robe to win back her husband's love.

The poison burned into his flesh in unbearable agony, driving Heracles to his funeral pyre, and Deianira, learning what she had done, took her own life in grief.

iolaus.name: Iolaus
iolaus.desc:
The nephew and devoted companion of Heracles, Iolaus served as the hero's charioteer and helper in many of his labours.

Most famously, it was he who seared the stumps of the Hydra's necks with fire as Heracles struck off its heads, so that no new head could grow — the crucial aid that let the hero overcome the otherwise unkillable monster.

eurystheus.name: Eurystheus
eurystheus.desc:
The king of Mycenae who set Heracles his twelve labours, Eurystheus gained his throne through Hera's scheming to rob Heracles of his birthright.

A cowardly and fearful king, he devised ever more impossible and deadly tasks for the hero, and was so terrified by the monsters Heracles brought back that he hid from them in a great bronze jar sunk in the earth.

phineus.name: Phineus
phineus.desc:
A blind seer and once-king cursed by the gods, Phineus was tormented by the Harpies, who swooped down to snatch and befoul his food at every meal, leaving him to starve amid plenty.

When the Argonauts came to him, the winged sons of the North Wind drove the Harpies away for good — and in gratitude the seer told the heroes how to pass safely through the clashing rocks.

harmonia.name: Harmonia
harmonia.desc:
The goddess of harmony and concord, Harmonia was the daughter of Ares and Aphrodite, given in marriage to Cadmus, founder of Thebes. Her wedding was attended by all the gods, but the necklace she received as a gift carried a curse that brought ruin on her descendants for generations.

In the end she and Cadmus were transformed into serpents and carried away to a blessed land.

epimetheus.name: Epimetheus
epimetheus.desc:
A Titan whose name means afterthought, Epimetheus is the scatter-brained brother of cunning Prometheus, forever acting before he thinks. When the gods fashioned the animals, he heedlessly gave away all the gifts — claws, fur, speed — leaving nothing for mankind, so that Prometheus had to steal fire to make up the lack.

Ignoring his brother's warning, he then accepted the gods' gift of Pandora, whose fatal jar loosed every ill upon the world.

pandora.name: Pandora
pandora.desc:
The first mortal woman, Pandora was fashioned by the gods on the orders of Zeus as a beautiful punishment for mankind after Prometheus stole fire. Each god gave her a gift — beauty, charm, cunning — and she was sent with a sealed jar to Epimetheus.

When her curiosity led her to open it, out flew every evil, toil and disease to plague the world forever, leaving only Hope trapped beneath the rim.

sisyphus.name: Sisyphus
sisyphus.desc:
The cunning and deceitful king of Corinth, Sisyphus was the craftiest of mortals, who twice cheated death itself — chaining up Thanatos so that none could die, and tricking his way back out of the underworld.

For his trickery and his affront to the gods, he was condemned to an eternity of futile labour: forever rolling a great boulder up a hill, only to watch it roll back down as it nears the top.

tantalus.name: Tantalus
tantalus.desc:
A king once favoured by the gods and admitted to their very table, Tantalus abused that honour terribly — stealing their nectar, and serving up his own son Pelops in a stew to test their sight.

For his crimes he was condemned to eternal torment in the underworld: standing in a pool that drains away when he stoops to drink, beneath fruit that lifts from his grasp when he reaches — forever tantalised by relief that never comes.

midas.name: Midas
midas.desc:
A king of Phrygia, Midas was granted by Dionysus a single wish, and foolishly asked that all he touched turn to gold. His delight curdled to horror when his food, his drink and even his own daughter hardened to cold metal at his touch, and he begged to be released, washing the curse away in a river.

In another tale he judged Pan a finer musician than Apollo, who gave him the ears of an ass for his poor taste.

narcissus.name: Narcissus
narcissus.desc:
A youth of extraordinary beauty, Narcissus was so proud that he scorned all who loved him, including the nymph Echo, who wasted away to a mere voice.

As punishment he was made to fall in love with his own reflection in a still pool, and, unable to tear himself from the unattainable image, he pined away and died there — becoming the flower that bears his name.

pygmalion.name: Pygmalion
pygmalion.desc:
A sculptor of Cyprus who despaired of mortal women, Pygmalion carved an ivory statue of such perfect beauty that he fell hopelessly in love with his own creation.

Praying to Aphrodite for a wife like his statue, he returned home to find the goddess had answered him — his kiss warmed the cold ivory to living flesh, and the statue-maiden became his bride.

ganymede.name: Ganymede
ganymede.desc:
The most beautiful of mortals, Ganymede was a Trojan prince so lovely that Zeus, smitten, took the form of an eagle to carry him up to Olympus. There he was made cupbearer to the gods, pouring their nectar in place of Hebe, and granted eternal youth and immortality.

He was set among the stars as the constellation Aquarius, forever a favourite of Zeus.

eurydice.name: Eurydice
eurydice.desc:
A nymph and the beloved wife of Orpheus, Eurydice died of a serpent's bite soon after their wedding. Her grieving husband followed her into the underworld and, by the beauty of his music, won her release — only to lose her a second time when, at the very threshold of the light, he turned to look back too soon.

She slipped away into the dark, and Orpheus mourned her all his days.

echo.name: Echo
echo.desc:
A mountain nymph cursed by Hera to repeat only the last words spoken to her, Echo fell hopelessly in love with the beautiful youth Narcissus.

Unable to speak her own heart and cruelly rejected, she wasted away in grief until nothing remained of her but her voice — the echo that still answers from lonely hills and hollow places.

daphne.name: Daphne
daphne.desc:
A nymph and daughter of a river-god, Daphne was pursued by the god Apollo, struck helplessly in love by one of Eros's arrows.

Fleeing his advances and desperate to keep her freedom, she prayed to her father for escape and was transformed into a laurel tree just as Apollo reached her — and the god thereafter wore its leaves as his sacred crown.

galatea.name: Galatea
galatea.desc:
A sea-nymph, one of the Nereids, Galatea was loved by the monstrous one-eyed Cyclops Polyphemus, whose clumsy songs of longing she scorned.

Her own heart belonged to the handsome shepherd Acis — and when the jealous Cyclops found them together, he crushed the youth beneath a boulder, and Galatea turned her dead lover's blood into a river that bears his name.

amphitrite.name: Amphitrite
amphitrite.desc:
The queen of the sea, Amphitrite is a sea-goddess and one of the Nereids, wife of Poseidon and mother of the merman Triton. Courted by Poseidon, she at first fled his advances into the deepest ocean, until a dolphin found her and won her over — for which the grateful god set the dolphin among the stars.

As mistress of the sea she stirs its creatures and calms or rouses its waves beside her husband.

aether.name: Aether
aether.desc:
The primordial god of the bright upper air, Aether is the pure, shining light of the heavens that the gods breathe, distinct from the common air of mortals below.

Child of Erebus the Darkness and Nyx the Night, he is the luminous atmosphere in which the stars and Olympus dwell — the shining boundary of the ordered world.

hemera.name: Hemera
hemera.desc:
The primordial goddess of the day, Hemera is the daylight that fills the world between the withdrawing and returning of her mother Night.

Daughter of Erebus and Nyx, she rises each morning as Nyx descends and returns each evening as her mother climbs back into the sky — the two forever passing at the threshold of the cosmos, never sharing the same house.

ourea.name: Ourea
ourea.desc:
The primordial gods of the mountains, the Ourea were among the very first beings, brought forth by Gaia the Earth of her own accord alongside the sky and the sea.

Ancient and elemental, they are less characters of story than the living presences of the mountain ranges themselves — the tall bones of the earth given divine form at the dawn of creation.

nereus.name: Nereus
nereus.desc:
The truthful old man of the sea, Nereus is a gentle, prophetic god of the calm depths, eldest son of Pontus and Gaia. Famed for his wisdom and honesty, he could change his shape at will to escape questioners — as he did when Heracles seized him to learn the way to the Garden of the Hesperides.

By the Oceanid Doris he fathered the fifty Nereids, the gentle nymphs of the sea, Thetis among them.

phorcys.name: Phorcys
phorcys.desc:
A primordial god of the sea's hidden dangers, Phorcys is a son of Pontus and Gaia, lord of the deep's monstrous and uncanny brood. With his sister-wife Ceto he fathered a fearsome line — the Gorgons, the Graeae, the serpent Echidna and others — so that from him descend many of the sea's terrors.

Often shown with a fish's tail and crab-claw forelegs, he embodies the deep's dark and dangerous power.

ceto.name: Ceto
ceto.desc:
A primordial goddess of the sea's dangers and its monsters, Ceto is a daughter of Pontus and Gaia whose very name means the great sea-beast.

With her brother-husband Phorcys she gave birth to a brood of horrors — the Gorgons, the Graeae, and other monsters of the deep — and so is mother to many of myth's most fearsome creatures.

proteus.name: Proteus
proteus.desc:
An old sea-god and herdsman of Poseidon's seals, Proteus is famed above all for two gifts — prophecy, and the power to change his shape into any form to avoid answering. To wring the truth from him one had to seize and hold him fast through every transformation — lion, serpent, water, fire — until, exhausted, he returned to his own shape and spoke true.

From him comes the word protean, for endless changeability.

triton.name: Triton
triton.desc:
The trumpeter of the sea, Triton is the merman son of Poseidon and Amphitrite, with the upper body of a man and the tail of a fish. He heralds the moods of the deep on a great twisted conch-shell, sounding it to raise the waves or calm them at his father's command.

A messenger of the sea-gods, he lends his name and form to the many lesser tritons who attend the ocean's processions.

styx.name: Styx
styx.desc:
The goddess of the great underworld river that bears her name, Styx is the eldest daughter of Oceanus, whose black waters wind seven times about the realm of the dead.

First to bring her children to Zeus's aid in the war against the Titans, she was honoured above all others — so that the most binding, unbreakable oath a god could swear was sworn upon her sacred waters.

crius.name: Crius
crius.desc:
A Titan of the southern heavens and the constellations, Crius is the least storied of the twelve Titans, known chiefly through his offspring. By Eurybia, a daughter of the sea, he fathered Astraeus (father of the stars and winds), Pallas and Perses — and so stands as ancestor to the powers of the night sky.

He too fought against Zeus and fell into Tartarus.

menoetius.name: Menoetius
menoetius.desc:
A Titan of violent rage and reckless pride, Menoetius was a son of Iapetus and brother of Atlas and Prometheus.

For his arrogance and insolent fury he was struck down by the thunderbolt of Zeus in the war of the gods and hurled into the darkness of Erebus — a byword for the hubris and violence that the new Olympian order crushed.

clymene.name: Clymene
clymene.desc:
An Oceanid nymph, Clymene was the wife of the Titan Iapetus and so mother of Atlas, Prometheus, Epimetheus and Menoetius — the ancestress, through them, of much of the fate of mankind.

In another line she was mother of Phaethon by the sun-god Helios, the reckless youth who begged to drive the sun-chariot and fell to his death.

eileithyia.name: Eileithyia
eileithyia.desc:
The goddess of childbirth and labour, Eileithyia is a daughter of Zeus and Hera who presides over the pains and safe delivery of every birth.

Her power to hasten or delay a birth made her an instrument of Hera's jealousy — most famously when the queen held her back to prolong the agony of Leto's labour, and to delay the birth of Heracles so another might steal his destined glory.

deimos.name: Deimos
deimos.desc:
The personification of terror and dread, Deimos is a son of Ares and Aphrodite and the twin brother of Phobos.

He rides at his father's side into the chaos of battle, spreading the paralysing fear that seizes soldiers in the face of slaughter — one of the grim spirits that attend the god of war upon the field.

phobos.name: Phobos
phobos.desc:
The personification of fear and panic, Phobos is a son of Ares and Aphrodite and the twin brother of Deimos.

He accompanies his father into battle, sowing the rout and flight that scatter armies, and his image was painted on shields and armour to strike dread into the enemy — the very face of terror in war.

morpheus.name: Morpheus
morpheus.desc:
The god of dreams, Morpheus is chief of the Oneiroi, the thousand sons of Sleep, and the shaper of the human forms that appear to sleepers in the night.

Able to take the shape and voice of any person, he brings messages and visions from the gods in dreams — the master of sleep's convincing illusions, from whom no dreamer can tell the false shape from the true.

erinyes.name: The Furies
erinyes.desc:
The Furies, dread goddesses of vengeance, the Erinyes rose from the blood of the castrated Uranus to punish the gravest of crimes — above all the murder of kin and the breaking of sacred oaths.

Relentless and terrible, with snakes for hair and eyes weeping blood, they hound the guilty to madness, as they pursued Orestes for the killing of his mother, until the gods themselves intervene.

charon.name: Charon
charon.desc:
The grim ferryman of the dead, Charon carries the souls of the newly deceased across the rivers Styx and Acheron into the underworld — but only those who have received proper burial rites and can pay his fare.

A coin was placed in the mouth of the dead for this passage; the unburied and the penniless were left to wander the near shore for a hundred years.

charites.name: The Graces
charites.desc:
The Graces, the Charites are goddesses of beauty, charm and the delights that make life sweet — usually three sisters: Aglaia (Splendour), Euphrosyne (Mirth) and Thalia (Good Cheer). Attendants of Aphrodite, they bring loveliness to feasts, dances and every joyful gathering, and lend their grace to art and to the beauty of the human form.

Wherever there is festivity, radiance or gladness, the Graces are said to preside.

pelops.name: Pelops
pelops.desc:
A prince of the house that bears his name, Pelops was as a child served up by his father Tantalus in a stew to test the gods, who restored him to life.

Grown, he won the princess Hippodamia in a deadly chariot race by sabotaging her father's chariot, then betrayed the accomplice who had helped him — bringing down the curse that would haunt his descendants, the doomed house of Atreus.

atreus.name: Atreus
atreus.desc:
A king of Mycenae and son of Pelops, Atreus was locked in a bitter feud with his brother Thyestes over the throne.

In the most infamous act of their blood-cursed house, he took revenge by killing his brother's sons and serving them to Thyestes at a banquet — a horror that deepened the curse descending upon his own sons, Agamemnon and Menelaus.

thyestes.name: Thyestes
thyestes.desc:
A prince of Mycenae and brother-rival of Atreus, Thyestes seized his brother's throne by treachery and was in turn made to eat his own murdered sons at a banquet set by Atreus.

Seeking vengeance, he fathered Aegisthus, who would grow up to help murder Agamemnon — carrying the curse of the house of Atreus into the next generation of bloodshed.

aegisthus.name: Aegisthus
aegisthus.desc:
The son of Thyestes, born to carry on his father's feud, Aegisthus seduced Clytemnestra while Agamemnon was away at Troy and helped her murder the returning king.
