When Zeus turned his lover Io into a white heifer to hide her, jealous Hera set the hundred-eyed giant Argus Panoptes to guard her — a watchman who never truly slept, for only some of his eyes ever closed at once. Zeus sent Hermes to free her, and the god lulled all hundred eyes to sleep with the drowsy music of his pipes and a long dull tale, then struck off the giant's head. In his memory, Hera set Argus's hundred eyes into the tail of her peacock.

Eros, the god of desire, is most often called the son of Aphrodite, and works as the instrument of his mother's power — loosing the arrows that make gods and mortals fall helplessly in love. Where Aphrodite is beauty and longing itself, Eros is the sharp, sudden strike of it, mother and son together ruling the whole domain of love.

Hermes fathered the goat-legged Pan, wild god of the shepherds' hills.

His mother is generally a nymph of Arcadia, and Hermes carried the goat-legged infant up to Olympus, where the gods were delighted with him — which is what the Homeric Hymn says his name means.

Iris the rainbow carries the messages of Hera between heaven, earth and sea.

Iris carries the messages of the Iliad while Hermes carries those of the Odyssey. She also fetches water from the Styx in a golden jug when a god must swear, which is the only errand no other deity will run.

Winged Nike, Victory, stands at the side of Zeus — the outcome he grants to whom he favours.

Styx brought her four children — Victory, Emulation, Power and Force — to Zeus at the outbreak of the Titan war, the first to declare for him. He gave them a permanent place beside him and made her waters the gods' binding oath.
The daughter of Zeus and Hera, Hebe poured the nectar of the gods as their cupbearer before she was given in marriage to the deified Heracles.
Hera's daughter Hebe, whose eternal youth she would later bestow on the deified Heracles as his bride.

Eris, Strife, and Ares, War, are siblings who walk the battlefield side by side.

Homer says Eris starts small and grows until her head is in the heavens while her feet are on the ground. It was her golden apple, thrown among the goddesses at the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, that started the war her brother enjoyed.
Nemesis answered the prayers of everyone Narcissus spurned — luring him to the still pool where he'd fall for his own reflection.

The nymph Echo, cursed by Hera to speak only the last words she heard, fell hopelessly in love with the beautiful youth Narcissus — yet could only echo his own words back, and he spurned her cruelly. She wasted away in grief until nothing remained of her but a voice. In punishment Narcissus was made to fall in love with his own reflection in a still pool, and there he pined away, unable to leave the image he could never hold, until he too withered into the flower that bears his name.

Eos the Dawn is a daughter of the Titan Hyperion and Theia.

Eos asked Zeus for immortality for her mortal lover Tithonus and forgot to ask for youth, so he aged without ever being able to die, and shrank at last into the cicada whose voice is all that is left of him.

Theia bore Eos, the rosy-fingered Dawn.

Aphrodite cursed her with insatiable desire for young men after finding her in bed with Ares, which is why the dawn goddess is always carrying someone off in the myths — Tithonus, Cephalus, Orion, Cleitus.

Eos the rosy-fingered Dawn and Helios the Sun are siblings, children of the Titans Hyperion and Theia. Each morning Eos rises first from the eastern sea and throws open the gates of the sky, and her brother's blazing chariot follows the path she has opened — dawn forever going before the day.

Eos the Dawn and Selene the Moon are sisters, daughters of the Titans Hyperion and Theia, and between them and their brother Helios the three divide the light of the sky. Selene drives her silver chariot through the night; Eos rises to end it, throwing open the eastern gates so that the darkness her sister ruled gives way to her brother's day.

Selene the Moon is a daughter of the Titan Hyperion, sister to the Sun and the Dawn.

She saw the shepherd Endymion asleep on Latmos and asked Zeus to keep him that way for ever, unaging and unconscious. She is said to have borne him fifty daughters, one for each month of the Olympiad, without waking him.

Theia bore Selene, the Moon.

Selene drives a chariot of two horses across the night as her brother drives four across the day, and the two are the timekeepers of the world before anyone was counting.

Helios the Sun and Selene the Moon, brother and sister, cross the heavens in turn.

They cross in turn and never together, and their sister Eos goes before them both. Odysseus's crew ate the cattle of Helios and the sun threatened to go down and shine among the dead instead — the one occasion the machinery is threatened with stopping.
Apollo fathered Asclepius and gave him to the wise centaur Chiron to raise — under whom the boy mastered a healing art that would one day rival death itself.
The wise centaur Chiron taught Asclepius medicine so thoroughly that the pupil learned to cheat death itself.

Asclepius, son of Apollo, grew so skilled in medicine that he could raise the dead — and when he did, Zeus saw the order of the world itself threatened, for if no one died the balance between gods and mortals would break. With a single thunderbolt he struck the healer down. Grief-stricken and enraged, Apollo could not touch Zeus, so he killed the Cyclopes who forged the bolt — and for that was sentenced to a year's servitude to a mortal king. Asclepius was later set among the stars.

Hypnos, gentle Sleep, is a son of Nyx the Night.

Hera bribed Hypnos to put Zeus to sleep so that the Greeks could be helped, and the price was one of the Graces as a wife. He had done it for her once before and been chased across the sky for it, and only escaped by taking refuge with his mother, whom Zeus did not dare offend.

Thanatos, Death, is a son of Nyx the Night and twin brother of Sleep.

Death was chained by Sisyphus so that no one on earth could die, and wrestled by Heracles at the tomb of Alcestis and made to give her back. He is the one power in the myths that mortals repeatedly, if briefly, beat.
Hypnos and Thanatos, Sleep and Death, are twin sons of Night — one a nightly rehearsal for the other.

Zeus fathered the nine Muses on Memory; Calliope, of epic song, was the eldest.

Zeus lay with Memory nine nights running near the summit of Olympus, and she bore the nine in a single birth. They sing at the feasts of the gods and supply mortals with everything anyone knows about them.

Calliope, chief of the Muses, is a daughter of Mnemosyne, Memory, by Zeus.

Calliope was asked to settle the quarrel between Aphrodite and Persephone over Adonis and divided the year between them, which is the same solution the gods reached over Persephone herself.
The three Fates, the Moirai, are daughters of Nyx the Night, outranking even the gods in the matter of destiny.
Chiron was Cronus's son by a nymph — which set him apart from the wild, violent centaurs as the wise and immortal one.

Chiron fed the boy Achilles on lions' marrow and taught him war, medicine and music alike.

Chiron raised Achilles after Thetis left, and taught Jason, Asclepius and Actaeon besides. Wounded incurably by one of Heracles's poisoned arrows and unable to die, he gave up his immortality to Prometheus and was released.
Chiron reared the exiled child Jason on Mount Pelion and schooled him for the throne he'd return to claim.

Ganymede, a Trojan prince, was the most beautiful of all mortal youths — so lovely that Zeus himself was smitten. In the form of a great eagle the god swept down and carried the boy up to Olympus, where he was made immortal and given the honoured office of cupbearer to the gods, pouring their nectar in Hebe's place. To his grieving father Zeus sent divine horses in recompense, and set Ganymede's likeness among the stars as the constellation Aquarius.
Zeus loved the priestess Io and, to hide her from Hera, turned her into a white heifer — which only began her sufferings.

Io was a priestess of Hera whom Zeus desired; caught in the act of seduction, Zeus turned her into a white heifer to hide the affair. But Hera, unfooled, demanded the heifer as a gift and set the hundred-eyed Argus to guard her. Even when Hermes killed the watchman and freed her, Hera sent a maddening gadfly to sting the heifer on and on, driving poor Io in torment across the whole world — a wandering that gave its name to the Ionian Sea and the Bosphorus, the 'ox-ford', before she found rest at last in Egypt.
Hundred-eyed Argus was set to watch the transformed Io night and day, so Zeus could never reach her.
Struck by Eros's arrow, Apollo pursued the nymph Daphne, who fled and was turned into a laurel tree — whose leaves the god took ever after as his crown.
Iapetus fathered Epimetheus, the heedless Titan whose afterthought left mankind defenceless and who took the fatal Pandora as his bride.
Prometheus and Epimetheus, Forethought and Afterthought, are brothers — one steals fire and foresees the cost, the other opens the door to Pandora.
Ignoring Prometheus's warning to refuse any gift from the gods, Epimetheus took Pandora as his wife — and her jar did the rest.
At Zeus's command, Hephaestus moulded Pandora, the first woman, from clay — beautiful, and bearing the jar of every human ill, the gods' revenge for stolen fire.

So cunning was Sisyphus that when Death came for him he asked Thanatos to show how his own chains worked — then snapped them shut, and no mortal died anywhere on earth until Ares came to free him. Caught again, Sisyphus had told his wife to leave his corpse unburied, then talked Persephone into letting him return briefly to rebuke her — and simply refused to go back. For cheating death twice he was condemned to roll a boulder up a hill forever, only to watch it roll back each time it neared the crest.

Tantalus, a son of Zeus admitted to the tables of the gods, betrayed that honour again and again — stealing their nectar and ambrosia for mortals, and, worst of all, killing his own son Pelops and serving him up as a feast to test whether the gods could tell. They knew at once. Their punishment was eternal: set in a pool that drained away whenever he bent to drink, beneath fruit that the wind swung out of reach whenever he grasped — forever hungry, forever thirsty, forever tantalised.

Midas sheltered the lost Silenus for ten days and returned him to Dionysus, who offered any reward he chose. He asked that everything he touched turn to gold.

The god granted it knowing what it meant, and released him once food, drink and — in Ovid — his own daughter had made the point. Midas washed the power off in the river Pactolus, which ran with gold ever after.
The sculptor Pygmalion loved his own ivory statue so purely that Aphrodite gave it life as the woman Galatea.
Moved by his devotion, Aphrodite answered Pygmalion's prayer and gave his ivory statue a beating heart.

When Poseidon sought the sea-nymph Amphitrite for his queen, she fled him into the farthest deeps of the ocean, wanting nothing to do with the god. But a dolphin found her hiding place and pleaded Poseidon's cause so sweetly that she relented and consented to be his bride. In gratitude Poseidon set the dolphin among the stars as a constellation, and Amphitrite reigned beside him as queen of the sea, mother of the merman Triton.
Aether the bright air is the child of Nyx the Night and her brother Erebus — light born, strangely, out of darkness.
Hemera the Day is Night's own daughter: as Nyx leaves the sky each dawn, Hemera enters it, and they never share it.
Aether the upper air and Hemera the Day are paired as the bright powers of the heavens, children together of the primordial dark.

Gaia the Earth brought forth Ourea, the mountains, from herself alone, as she did the sea and sky.

Gaia produced the mountains, the sea and the sky out of herself without a partner, before any pairing existed. The Ourea have no myths of their own; they are the world's furniture appearing as it is made.

Nereus, the gentle 'Old Man of the Sea', is the eldest son of Pontus the Deep and Gaia the Earth.

Heracles caught the old sea-god asleep and held him through every shape he took until he gave up the location of the golden apples. It is the same technique Menelaus used on Proteus — the sea tells the truth only under restraint.

Phorcys, god of the sea's hidden perils, is a son of Pontus the Deep and Gaia.

Phorcys and his sister Ceto between them produce almost every monster the heroes have to kill, so the danger of the sea is genealogically the danger of the world.

Ceto, mother of sea-monsters, is a daughter of Pontus the Deep and Gaia the Earth.

Her name is simply the word for a sea-monster, and the beast Perseus killed at Andromeda's rock is called by it. The mother and her offspring are barely distinguished in the language.
Phorcys and his sister Ceto together spawned the sea's monstrous brood — the Gorgons, the Graeae and the serpent Echidna among them.

Medusa the Gorgon is a daughter of the sea-gods Phorcys and Ceto.

Alone of the three sisters Medusa was born mortal, which is the only reason the raid was possible. Perseus needed a mirror-bright shield, winged sandals and a cap of invisibility to kill something that could in principle be killed.

Ceto, goddess of sea-monsters, mothered the Gorgon Medusa with Phorcys.

Athena had turned her into a monster for lying with Poseidon in her temple, and took the head afterwards for the front of her aegis, where it kept the power to petrify. The punishment and the trophy are the same object.

The grey Graeae are daughters of Phorcys and Ceto, sisters and wardens of their kin the Gorgons.

They were born grey-haired and shared a single eye and a single tooth between the three of them. Perseus took the eye as it passed from hand to hand and would not return it until they told him where to find the nymphs who held his equipment.

Ceto bore the Graeae, three grey sisters with a single shared eye, alongside her Gorgon daughters.

The Graeae are the Gorgons' sisters and their wardens, set on the road to the place where the mortal one could be found. Making them the only route in is what turns the killing of Medusa into a puzzle rather than a fight.
Nereus, the truthful old man of the sea, fathered the fifty Nereids — Thetis, mother of Achilles, chief among them.

Amphitrite, queen of the sea, is a Nereid daughter of Nereus.

Poseidon pursued her and she fled to Atlas at the far edge of the sea. A dolphin found her and argued his case so well that she consented, and Poseidon set the creature among the stars for it.

Triton the merman is the son of Poseidon and Amphitrite, herald of his father's sea.

Triton blows a conch to raise or calm the waves at his father's order, and it was that horn, sounded at Zeus's command, that told the flood waters to withdraw after Deucalion.

Proteus the shape-shifting seer serves Poseidon as herdsman of his seals in the deep.

He knows everything that happens in the sea and will say none of it willingly, which is why every encounter with him is a wrestling match. Menelaus got home only by holding him through lion, serpent, water and tree.

Styx, eldest of the underworld rivers, is a daughter of the Titan Oceanus and Tethys.

Styx was the first of all the gods to come to Zeus's side in the war, bringing her four children with her. He rewarded her by making her water the oath that no god can break — a perjured immortal lies breathless for a year and is exiled for nine more.

Tethys mothered the river-goddess Styx, whose waters bind even the gods' oaths.

The river runs through the underworld and the oath runs through the whole pantheon, so a daughter of the Titans holds the one instrument that binds the Olympians who replaced them.
When Zeus rose against the Titans, Styx was the first to bring her children to his side; in thanks he made her name the oath no god dares break.

Crius the Titan of the constellations is a son of Uranus the Sky and Gaia the Earth.

Crius is the least characterised of the twelve Titans, defined almost entirely by descendants — through his sons come the winds, the stars, the dawn's husband, and the Titaness Hecate.

Gaia bore the Titan Crius, whose line would include the stars, the winds and the dawn.

He held the southern corner of the sky at the castration of Uranus and was imprisoned in Tartarus after the war, along with every other Titan who had fought.

Menoetius the violent is a son of Iapetus, and brother to Atlas and Prometheus.

Menoetius is destroyed in a line and a half of the Theogony: Zeus struck him with a thunderbolt for his outrageous pride and his reckless strength, and sent him down to Erebus. He does nothing else in the surviving literature.

The Oceanid Clymene bore Menoetius to Iapetus, alongside Atlas and Prometheus.

Clymene's four sons are the tests of a single idea — Prometheus thinks ahead and endures, Epimetheus thinks late and is caught, Atlas is punished with labour and Menoetius simply obliterated.
For his reckless violence in the war of the gods, Zeus struck Menoetius down with a thunderbolt into the dark of Erebus.

The Titan Iapetus and the Oceanid Clymene are the parents of Prometheus, Atlas and Epimetheus.

Some accounts substitute the Oceanid Asia for Clymene as the mother of the four, and Aeschylus makes Prometheus a son of Themis instead. The disagreement matters because it decides whether the fire-bringer is a Titan's son or a goddess of law's.

Prometheus the forethinker is the son of Iapetus and the Oceanid Clymene.

He sided with Zeus in the war against his own kin, and was punished later for helping mortals instead — fire hidden in a fennel stalk, and the sacrifice rigged so that men kept the meat and the gods got the bones.

Atlas, who holds up the sky, is a son of Iapetus and Clymene.

Atlas fought against Zeus and was given the sky to hold rather than Tartarus, a sentence designed to be visible. Heracles took the weight briefly and Atlas fetched the golden apples, then had to be tricked into taking it back.
Eileithyia, goddess of childbirth, is the daughter of Zeus and Hera — and the very help Hera withholds from Zeus's other loves in labour.
Hera's daughter Eileithyia eases childbirth; Hera commands her to delay the births of her husband's rivals.
Deimos, Terror, is the son of Ares the war-god and Aphrodite, and rides at his father's side into battle.

Aphrodite bore Deimos, Terror, to Ares — love and war together fathering panic.

Deimos and Phobos ride with their father in the Iliad and yoke his horses. Terror and Rout are the whole content of the war-god's household — he has no counsellors and no cult of note, only the panic he causes.

Phobos, Fear, is a son of Ares and Aphrodite, the dread that scatters armies before his father.

Agamemnon's shield carries the Gorgon flanked by Terror and Rout, and Phobos appears on the shield of Achilles too. Fear is the thing armies actually break under, so it is fear that gets painted on the equipment.

Aphrodite mothered Phobos, Fear, with the war-god Ares.

That love and war produce Fear, Terror and Harmony between them is the neatest piece of theological argument in the genealogies — the same pairing yields both the panic of the battlefield and the concord of the wedding.
Deimos and Phobos, Terror and Fear, are twin sons of Ares and Aphrodite who haunt every battlefield together.

Morpheus, who shapes the figures of dreams, is a son of Hypnos the Sleep.

Morpheus takes the shapes of people in dreams, and his brothers take the shapes of animals and of objects, so the whole content of a dream is divided between three sons of Sleep. Ovid supplies the scheme; earlier sources do not name him.
The Furies sprang from the blood of Uranus when Cronus unmanned him — vengeance itself born of that first violence.
Charon ferries the dead across the Styx into the realm of Hades, taking his fee in the coins left with the dead.

The three Graces, who lend beauty and joy, are daughters of Zeus.

The three Graces attend Aphrodite, weave the robes of the gods, and give whatever charm a thing has beyond its usefulness. Hera promised one of them to Hypnos as the price for putting Zeus to sleep.
The Graces attend Aphrodite, dressing and adorning the goddess of beauty as her constant companions.

Stheno the immortal Gorgon is a daughter of the sea-gods Phorcys and Ceto, and sister to Medusa.

Stheno is credited with killing more men than either of her sisters, though she has no story of her own. The Gorgons work as a set: two immortal and undefeatable, one mortal and therefore the plot.

Euryale the immortal Gorgon is Ceto's daughter and Medusa's sister.

Pindar makes the sound of Euryale's grief the origin of the aulos: Athena heard the sisters wailing over Medusa and set the sound to music, inventing the double pipe to reproduce it.
Stheno and Euryale are Medusa's deathless Gorgon sisters; only Medusa could be slain, and Perseus slew her.

Euryale is Medusa's immortal sister, whose wail of grief follows Perseus's killing stroke.

Perseus escaped the two immortal sisters only by the cap of invisibility, since nothing else would have saved him. They could pursue him for ever and never catch or avenge, which is why the story lets them fall behind.

Stheno and Euryale, the two immortal Gorgons, guard the memory of their slain sister Medusa.

Neither can die and neither can be avenged, so their part of the story simply stops when Perseus disappears. Their immortality, which should be an advantage, is what makes them powerless in the narrative.

To find the road to Medusa, Perseus first had to wring the secret from the Graeae — three grey witches, sisters of the Gorgons, old since birth, who shared a single eye and a single tooth between them, passing them from hand to hand. Perseus watched and waited, and at the very moment the eye was being handed across, he snatched it away. Blind and helpless, the sisters could only bargain: to win back their one eye they told him where to find the nymphs who kept the weapons he would need.
The grey Graeae kept the secret road to their sisters the Gorgons, Medusa among them, until Perseus forced it from them.

For his tenth labour Heracles journeyed to the far western edge of the world to seize the cattle of Geryon — a monster with three bodies joined at the waist, three heads, six arms. To reach him he crossed the ocean in the golden cup of the Sun, and on the way raised the great Pillars that bear his name at the strait. He slew the herdsman and the two-headed hound Orthrus, then felled Geryon with a single arrow, poisoned with the Hydra's blood, that pierced all three bodies at once.

Orthrus was a two-headed hound — brother to Cerberus, born of the monsters Typhon and Echidna — set to guard the red cattle of Geryon at the western edge of the world. When Heracles came to carry off the herd for his tenth labour, the beast rushed him, and he felled it with a single blow of his olivewood club before turning on its master. It was the first of the guardians of Geryon's cattle to fall.

The two-headed dog Orthrus guarded the cattle of the giant Geryon until Heracles came for the herd.

Geryon had three bodies joined at the waist and kept red cattle on an island in the far west, guarded by the herdsman Eurytion and the two-headed dog. Heracles killed all three to take the herd on the tenth labour.

Orthrus the two-headed hound is another of Echidna's monstrous brood, brother to Cerberus.

Orthrus dies in a sentence, clubbed on the way to the cattle. In Hesiod he then fathers the Sphinx and the Nemean Lion on his own mother, which makes the monster genealogy fold back on itself.

For his fourth labour Heracles was ordered to bring the monstrous Erymanthian Boar back alive — a beast that ravaged the mountain slopes. He chased it up into the high snows, where its heavy body floundered in the drifts, then sprang upon it, bound it fast in chains, and hauled it onto his shoulders. When he carried the living, thrashing boar into the court of King Eurystheus, who had set him the labours, the terrified king dived into a great bronze jar to hide and shouted his orders from inside it.

For his sixth labour Heracles faced the Stymphalian Birds — a vast flock of man-eating creatures with bronze beaks, metallic feathers they could loose like arrows, and poisonous dung, that had gathered in a marsh too soft to cross on foot or by boat. Athena gave him a great bronze rattle forged by Hephaestus; its clashing din startled the birds up into the air in a screaming cloud, and there Heracles shot them down with his arrows as they flew, and drove the survivors from Greece forever.

The third labour asked not for slaughter but for patience: to capture the Ceryneian Hind alive, a deer sacred to Artemis with golden antlers and hooves of bronze, swifter than an arrow. Unwilling to harm a creature of the goddess, Heracles pursued it on foot for a full year, across mountains and rivers to the edge of the world, until at last he caught it — and when Artemis rose in anger to stop him, he explained the labour laid on him, and she let him carry the hind away unhurt.
The golden Hind is sacred to Artemis, who nearly punishes Heracles until he shows he took it alive and unharmed.

For his seventh labour Heracles sailed to Crete to capture the great Bull that Poseidon had sent from the sea — the same beast that had fathered the Minotaur upon Queen Pasiphae, and now ran wild ravaging the island. King Minos offered help, but Heracles took it alone: he wrestled the raging bull down with his bare hands, subdued it, and shipped it back across the water to Greece. Released afterward, it wandered north to the plain of Marathon, to trouble heroes yet to come.

The Cretan Bull, sent by Poseidon, rampaged over Minos's Crete until Heracles removed it.

Minos kept the bull rather than sacrificing it, and everything that followed came from that: his wife's passion, the Minotaur, the labyrinth, the Athenian tribute and Theseus. One withheld offering generates the whole Cretan cycle.

Poseidon sent the bull ashore from the sea as a sign that Minos should sacrifice it to him. When Minos kept the beast for his herds and offered a lesser animal instead, the god turned it savage and set it rampaging across Crete.

The same slight drove Poseidon to make Pasiphae desire the bull, so the Minotaur was the second half of one punishment.

Telamon fought beside Heracles in an earlier sack of Troy and sailed with him among the Argonauts.

Heracles sacked Troy a generation before the war, over Laomedon's refusal to pay for rescuing his daughter, and gave Telamon the princess Hesione as his prize. Her captivity was still being cited by the Trojans as a grievance when the Greeks arrived.

Tantalus, testing whether the gods were truly all-knowing, killed his son Pelops, cooked him, and served the flesh at a feast. The gods saw through it at once and refused the meal — all but grieving Demeter, who absently ate the shoulder. They restored Pelops to life and gave him a shoulder of gleaming ivory to replace the eaten piece, while Tantalus was damned to his eternal hunger and thirst in the underworld.

Pelops, as a boy, had been served up by his father Tantalus as a meal to test the gods — and though the others recoiled, Demeter distractedly ate his shoulder. The gods restored the boy to life, fashioning a shoulder of ivory to replace the eaten one, and he emerged more beautiful than before. So lovely was he that Poseidon fell in love with him, carried him up to Olympus, and later, when Pelops raced for a bride, gave him a chariot drawn by winged horses to win her.

Atreus, whose house the family curse would tear apart, is a son of Pelops.

Pelops had won his bride by bribing a charioteer and then killing him, and the dying man's curse ran through the house — Atreus and Thyestes, Agamemnon and Aegisthus, Orestes and Clytemnestra, three generations of it.

Thyestes, rival to his brother Atreus, is a son of Pelops.

The brothers began by conspiring together to murder their half-brother Chrysippus and were exiled for it. Everything they later did to each other repeats that first collaboration in reverse.
Atreus took revenge on his brother Thyestes by serving him his own murdered sons at a banquet — the crime at the black heart of their house's curse.

Atreus took revenge on his brother Thyestes by serving him a feast of his own murdered sons.

Thyestes had seduced Atreus's wife and stolen the golden lamb that carried the kingship. Atreus served him his own children at a reconciliation feast and showed him the hands and heads afterwards.

Agamemnon, who leads the Greeks to Troy, is a son of Atreus of Mycenae.

Agamemnon inherits the kingship, the curse and the quarrel: Aegisthus, the surviving son of the brother Atreus fed his own children to, was waiting in Mycenae the whole ten years he was at Troy.

Menelaus, whose wife Helen was carried to Troy, is a son of Atreus and brother of Agamemnon.

Menelaus gets the gentler share of the inheritance — Helen recovered, no murder waiting at home, and an eventual translation to Elysium because he was Zeus's son-in-law rather than for anything he did.
Aegisthus, who murders Agamemnon, is the surviving son of Thyestes — the family's revenge made flesh.
While Agamemnon warred at Troy, Aegisthus became the lover of his wife Clytemnestra and her partner in his murder.
Aegisthus, avenging his father Thyestes, helps Clytemnestra cut down Agamemnon on his return from Troy.
Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia to win fair winds for Troy — the crime that turned his wife into his murderer.

Becalmed at Aulis, the Greek fleet could not sail for Troy until Agamemnon appeased Artemis — and the price the goddess named was his own daughter. He lured Iphigenia to the camp with the promise of marriage to Achilles, then gave her to the altar-knife so the winds would rise. Some say Artemis snatched her away at the last moment and left a deer in her place; but the deed, or the willingness to do it, poisoned his house forever and armed his wife's revenge.
Clytemnestra never forgave Agamemnon for sacrificing their daughter Iphigenia; it is the root of her revenge.
In the kinder tellings, Artemis snatches Iphigenia from the altar at the last instant, leaving a deer in her place.

Orestes is the son who avenges Agamemnon by killing the murderers — including his own mother.

Clytemnestra killed Agamemnon on his return, and Apollo required Orestes to avenge him by killing her. The Furies pursued him for it until Athena convened the first homicide court at Athens and split the vote in his favour.
Electra keeps alive the memory of her murdered father Agamemnon and goads her brother Orestes to revenge.

Orestes is Clytemnestra's son — and, avenging his father, her killer; the Furies hunt him for it.

Aeschylus gives her the strongest scene in the trilogy when she bares her breast to him and asks whether he can kill the body that nursed him. He hesitates, Pylades reminds him of Apollo's command, and he does it.

Driven by Apollo's command to avenge his father, Orestes returned in secret to Mycenae and killed his mother Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus — paying blood for blood. But to murder a mother, however just the cause, was a crime the Furies could not forgive: they rose from the earth and hounded him mad across Greece, until at last Athena herself convened a court in Athens to judge him, and cast the deciding vote for mercy — ending the family's long chain of vengeance.
Orestes cuts down Aegisthus, his father's murderer and his mother's lover, in taking the family's revenge.

Electra, daughter of Clytemnestra, sides wholly with her murdered father and against her mother.

Electra was kept in the house, married off to a peasant in one version to keep her line harmless, and she waited years for her brother. All three tragedians wrote her, and in each she is more relentless than Orestes.
Orestes and Electra, children of Agamemnon, join to avenge their father on their mother and her lover.
The Furies hound Orestes to madness for the blood of his mother, until the gods at last grant him release.
Priam, last king of Troy, is a son of Laomedon, whose broken word to the gods first brought ruin on the city.
Poseidon built Troy's walls for Laomedon and, cheated of his pay, sent a sea-monster against the city.

King Laomedon of Troy had cheated the gods, refusing Poseidon and Apollo their wages for building his walls — so Poseidon sent a sea-monster to ravage the coast, and only the sacrifice of the king's daughter could appease it. Heracles offered to slay the beast in return for Laomedon's divine horses; he killed it, but the king cheated him too and withheld the reward. Enraged, Heracles came back with an army, sacked Troy, killed Laomedon and all his sons but one — sparing only young Priam, who would live to see the city fall a second time.
Priam and Hecuba are king and queen of Troy, parents of Hector, Paris and Cassandra, who outlive nearly all their children.

Hector, Troy's great defender, is the son of Priam and Hecuba.

Hecuba bore nineteen of Priam's fifty sons and lost most of them to Achilles. She appeals to Hector from the wall to come inside, baring her breast to remind him she nursed him, and he stays out and dies.

Paris, whose theft of Helen doomed Troy, is a son of Priam and Hecuba.

Hecuba dreamed she gave birth to a burning torch, and the seers said the child would destroy the city. He was exposed on Ida, raised by shepherds, and came back to Troy as a young man and was recognised and welcomed.

Cassandra, the prophetess no one believes, is a daughter of Priam and Hecuba.

Apollo gave her true prophecy to win her and, refused, added the curse that no one would believe her. She told Troy about Paris, the Greeks' ships and the wooden horse, and was ignored each time.

Hecuba's daughter Cassandra foresees Troy's fall clearly, and is believed by no one.

After the sack Hecuba saw Cassandra taken by Agamemnon, her daughter Polyxena killed on Achilles's tomb, and her last son murdered by the guest-friend he had been sent to for safety. Euripides gives her the revenge and the transformation into a dog.
Apollo gave Cassandra true prophecy to win her love; when she refused him, he cursed the gift so none would ever believe her.

Cassandra, princess of Troy, had been given the gift of true prophecy by Apollo — and when she spurned him, the curse that no one would ever believe her. She foresaw the fall of Troy and was mocked; foresaw her own death and could not prevent it. Taken as a war-prize by Agamemnon when the city fell, she was carried to Mycenae, where she foretold that both she and the king would be murdered the moment they crossed the threshold — and walked in knowing it, to the axe of Clytemnestra.

Cassandra foresaw the death of her brother Hector and the fall of the city, and was mocked for it.

She was the first to see her father bringing Hector's body back from the Greek camp, and it is her cry from the walls that brings the whole city out to meet it in the last book of the Iliad.
Aphrodite bore the hero Aeneas to the mortal Anchises, and shielded her son through the fall of Troy and his fated journey to found a new nation.
Anchises fathered Aeneas with the goddess Aphrodite, and is carried from burning Troy on his son's back.

Weary of Aphrodite forever making the gods fall for mortals, Zeus struck her with desire for one herself: Anchises, a handsome Trojan prince herding his cattle on Mount Ida. Disguised as a mortal maiden she came to him and lay with him — then revealed her godhead and told him she would bear his son, the hero Aeneas, but warned him never to boast of bedding a goddess. When at last, in his cups, he did, a bolt from Zeus lamed him for the rest of his days.

Aphrodite shields her son Aeneas through the war and out of falling Troy toward a new destiny.

She carries him out of the fighting when Diomedes attacks him and is wounded in the wrist for it, the only goddess in the Iliad to be hurt while shielding a son. Her protection is what lets the Trojan line survive the city.

Thetis was married to the mortal hero Peleus against her will — a sea-goddess given to a man because a prophecy warned that her son would outshine his father, too dangerous a bride for any god. Their wedding drew all the Olympians, and it was there that the uninvited Eris rolled in the golden apple 'for the fairest,' setting in motion the quarrel that led to the Trojan War. From the reluctant union came Achilles.
Peleus wed the sea-nymph Thetis, and from that union — attended by all the gods — came Achilles, the greatest warrior of the age.

The centaur Chiron fostered and taught Peleus, and later his son Achilles, on Mount Pelion.

Chiron taught Peleus, saved him when he was left weaponless on Pelion, and arranged his marriage to Thetis by telling him how to hold her through her changes of shape.

Great Ajax, the bulwark of the Greeks, is the son of Telamon.

Ajax needs no divine help and gets none: the largest shield in the army, the man who holds the line while Achilles sulks, and the one who kills himself when Achilles's armour is awarded to Odysseus instead.
Neoptolemus is brought to Troy after his father Achilles' death to help finish the war his father could not.
Philoctetes lit the pyre that freed the dying Heracles, and received the great bow of Heracles as his reward.
Odysseus, who had helped maroon the wounded Philoctetes, is sent to coax him and the bow of Heracles back to win the war.
Odysseus fetches the young Neoptolemus, son of Achilles, to Troy, knowing the city cannot fall without him.
Palamedes exposed Odysseus's feigned madness to force him to Troy; Odysseus never forgave him and framed him for treason.

When the kings came to muster Odysseus for the war at Troy, he feigned madness to stay home — until Palamedes exposed the ruse by setting his infant son before his plough, forcing him to swerve and prove his wits sound. Odysseus never forgave the humiliation. Later at Troy he took his revenge by forging a treasonous letter and planting gold in Palamedes's tent, framing him as a traitor bought by the Trojans — and the innocent man was stoned to death by his own comrades.
Anticlea is the mother of Odysseus; she dies of longing in his absence, and he meets her weeping shade in the land of the dead.
Laertes and Anticlea are the parents of Odysseus; she dies of grief while he wanders and her husband withdraws to his orchard.
The old nurse Eurycleia raised Odysseus and, washing the beggar's feet, knows him by his scar — and keeps his secret.
Odysseus's old hound Argos, neglected for twenty years, lifts his head to know his disguised master, then dies content.
Aeolus, keeper of the winds, feasts Odysseus and gives him the storms tied in a bag — which his crew open in sight of Ithaca.
Elpenor, youngest of the crew, falls drunk from Circe's roof; his unburied shade begs Odysseus for a proper grave.
Eurylochus, Odysseus's second, alone escapes Circe's spell to warn him — then later leads the fatal feast on Helios's cattle.
Against Odysseus's warning, Eurylochus urges the starving crew to slaughter the cattle of Helios — the sin that dooms them all.

Semele, mother of Dionysus, is a daughter of Cadmus, founder of Thebes.

Cadmus founded Thebes and his daughters brought it down: Semele burned, Agave tore her son apart, Ino leapt into the sea. Their nephew Pentheus and their great-grandson Oedipus complete the ruin of the house.

Ino, who nurses the infant Dionysus, is a daughter of Cadmus and sister of Semele.

Ino nursed the infant Dionysus and was driven mad by Hera for it. She leapt into the sea with her son and was made the sea-goddess Leucothea, who in the Odyssey gives Odysseus the veil that keeps him afloat.

Agave, who will tear apart her own son, is a daughter of Cadmus and sister of Semele.

Agave denied that her sister Semele had lain with Zeus and said the story was a cover for an ordinary seduction. The god's answer was to send her onto the mountain in madness to tear her own son apart with her hands.
Ino takes in her sister Semele's orphaned son Dionysus and nurses him, drawing Hera's wrath upon herself.
Ino nursed the infant Dionysus after Semele's death, and was driven mad and into the sea by Hera for it.
Hera, hating the child Dionysus, struck his aunt and nurse Ino with a madness that drove her leaping into the sea.
Pentheus, who denies Dionysus, is the son of Agave — and dies torn apart by her own hands in the god's frenzy.

Pentheus, King of Thebes, refused to honour the new god Dionysus — his own cousin — and tried to cage him and outlaw his rites. So the god clouded his mind and lured him, disguised as a woman, to spy on the revels on the mountain. There the frenzied worshippers, led by Pentheus's own mother Agave, took him for a wild beast and fell upon him. Agave tore off her son's head with her bare hands and carried it home in triumph — waking from the god's spell only when she saw what she held.
In the madness sent by Dionysus, Agave tore her son Pentheus limb from limb, mistaking him for a lion.

King Pentheus set himself against his cousin the god Dionysus, and was destroyed for it.

Pentheus refused to admit that his cousin was a god and tried to imprison him. Dionysus led him out to spy on the women in a dress, and his own mother, in the god's madness, tore his head off believing him a lion.

The hunter Actaeon, ranging the woods with his hounds, stumbled by chance upon Artemis bathing naked in a sacred spring. Enraged that a mortal had seen her, the virgin goddess flung water in his face and turned him into a stag — leaving his human mind trapped inside the beast. His own fifty hunting dogs, no longer knowing their master, fell upon him and tore him apart, while he could only weep and could not call out their names.

Eteocles, who seizes Thebes and dies fighting his brother, is a son of Oedipus.

The brothers agreed to rule Thebes in alternate years and Eteocles refused to give up his turn, which brought Polynices back with an Argive army. They killed each other in single combat at the seventh gate.

Polynices, who brings an army against Thebes and dies by his brother's hand, is a son of Oedipus.

Oedipus cursed both sons for their treatment of him, and at Colonus refused Polynices even after he came to beg for support. The curse was that they should divide their inheritance with the sword.

Ismene, the more cautious sister, is a daughter of Oedipus and sister of Antigone.

Ismene brings news from Thebes to her father and sister at Colonus and is captured by Creon there. She survives the play she is in and is never mentioned again, which is the closest anyone in the family gets to an ending.

The two sons of Oedipus agreed to share Thebes by ruling in alternate years — but when his term ended, Eteocles refused to yield the throne, and Polynices raised an army of seven champions to take it by force. In the war's last duel the brothers met before the gates and ran each other through in the same instant, each dying by the other's hand — fulfilling their blind father's curse that they would divide their inheritance with the sword.
Eteocles and Polynices agreed to share Thebes and did not; their quarrel brings seven armies to the walls and both to death.
Antigone defies the king's decree to bury her brother Polynices, and is condemned to death for the loyalty.
Antigone and Ismene are Oedipus's daughters; Antigone goes to her death for burying their brother while the fearful Ismene holds back.
Antigone mourns both her brothers, though the king permits burial only for Eteocles and not for Polynices.
Creon forbids the burial of Polynices as a traitor, leaving his body to rot — the decree Antigone dies defying.

When Antigone's brother Polynices fell attacking Thebes, King Creon decreed that the traitor's body lie unburied for the dogs and crows, on pain of death. But Antigone, holding the law of the gods above the law of the king, crept out and scattered earth over her brother's corpse. Caught and unrepentant, she was sealed alive in a tomb by Creon's order — where she hanged herself. His son Haemon, her betrothed, fell on his own sword beside her, and Creon was left to grief and ruin.
Haemon, betrothed to Antigone, is the son of Creon — and kills himself over her body, breaking his father.

Haemon is betrothed to Antigone and dies beside her when his father Creon condemns her.

Haemon argues with his father in the play's central scene, telling him that the city sympathises with the girl and that a man who cannot listen should not rule. Creon relents too late and finds him already dead in the tomb.
Creon is the brother of Jocasta; he takes the throne of Thebes after the fall of her son and husband Oedipus.
Zeus saved the unborn Dionysus from his mother's ashes and sheltered him from Hera's fury until he could take his place among the gods.
At Zeus's command, Hermes carried the infant Dionysus to safety, away from Hera, to be raised in secret.

Athena stands by Heracles through his Labours, lending counsel and arms to her favourite mortal.

She hands him the bronze rattles that startle the Stymphalian birds off the marsh, holds up the sky beside him, and leads him into Olympus at the end. Hera sent his madness and his labours; Athena is the counterweight throughout.
Hermes equips and guides Heracles, even leading him down to fetch Cerberus from the land of the dead.
The wise centaur Chiron schooled Peleus and gave him the ashen spear that his son Achilles would carry to Troy.

Circe, the enchantress of Aiaia who turned Odysseus's men into swine, was a daughter of Helios, and the sun's fire runs in her. Her golden loom, her knowledge of drugs and transformations, and the uncanny light of her island all mark her as the Titan sun's child — a divinity of dangerous, radiant power.

Circe and Aeetes, the sorcerer-king of Colchis who guarded the Golden Fleece, were both children of Helios, and both inherited the sun's dangerous magic. She turned men to beasts on her island; he set the deadly tasks that Jason could only survive with Medea's — Aeetes's own daughter's — help. Together the siblings mark a whole bloodline of solar enchanters.
The sleepless Colchian Dragon guarded the Golden Fleece until Medea lulled it to sleep, letting Jason seize the prize at last.

The Golden Fleece hung in a sacred grove in Colchis, guarded by a dragon that never slept, its coils wound about the tree. Jason could never have passed it by strength — but Medea, the king's daughter and a priestess of Hecate, had fallen in love with him. In the dark she led him to the grove and worked her sorcery: sprinkling the beast with a drugged potion and singing charms of sleep until at last the unsleeping dragon's eyes closed, and Jason lifted the Fleece from the tree unharmed.

As the Argo fled Colchis with the Golden Fleece it came to Crete — guarded by Talos, a giant of bronze forged by Hephaestus, who circled the island three times a day and hurled boulders at any ship that neared. He had but one vein, running from neck to ankle and sealed by a single bronze nail. The sorceress Medea bewitched him with her arts and drew the nail out; the divine ichor that was his lifeblood ran from him like molten lead, and the bronze giant crashed lifeless to the shore.
The bronze giant Talos circled Crete three times a day to guard King Minos's shores, until Medea undid him.

Nike, winged victory, is the daughter of the river Styx by the Titan Pallas.

Styx brought Victory, Emulation, Power and Force to Zeus before the fighting began, and the four of them have stood beside his throne ever since. Choosing early is the reason the family kept its privileges under the new regime.

Helios the sun is the son of the Titan Hyperion by his sister Theia.

Helios sees everything from above and is the witness the other gods call: he told Demeter who had taken Persephone, and told Hephaestus where to find Ares and Aphrodite.

Theia, Titaness of light, bore Helios, Selene and Eos to Hyperion.

He let his son Phaethon drive the chariot for a day and had to watch Zeus strike him out of the sky with a thunderbolt before the earth burned. Helios threatened to stop driving altogether, and had to be talked round.

Calypso was a daughter of the Titan Atlas, who bears the weight of the sky on his shoulders, and something of his lonely endurance marks her. On her remote island of Ogygia she kept Odysseus for seven years, offering him immortality if he would stay — a Titan's child holding a mortal against the pull of home, until the gods themselves ordered her to let him go.

Eris, strife incarnate, is a daughter born of Night alone.

Night's children in the Theogony are all the things that come without a father — Doom, Fate, Death, Sleep, Blame, Misery, the Fates, Retribution, Deceit, Old Age and Strife. Eris is the one who does the most narrative work.

Nemesis, who apportions retribution, is a daughter of Night.

Nemesis attends prosperity to make sure it does not exceed itself. In one tradition she, not Leda, was pursued by Zeus in the form of a swan and laid the egg from which Helen came, which makes the Trojan War a retribution by descent.

Echidna, mother of monsters, is a child of the old sea-gods Phorcys and Ceto.

Hesiod places her in a cave under a rock, half beautiful woman and half enormous serpent, ageless and deathless. Almost every creature the heroes fight is her child by Typhon.

Ceto, goddess of the sea's terrors, bore Echidna, half-woman and half-serpent.

Some readings of the Theogony give her different parents — Callirhoe and Chrysaor — and the ambiguity has never been resolved. Either way she stands between the sea-gods and the monsters as the point where one becomes the other.

The Furies rose from the blood of the castrated Uranus where it fell upon Gaia.

They were born of the blood that fell on the earth when Cronus castrated Uranus, so the Furies who pursue kin-murderers are themselves the issue of the first crime within a family.

Charon, ferryman of the dead, is a son of Night and Darkness.

He takes an obol from each mouth and refuses anyone unburied, which is why the dead in the poems beg so urgently for their rites: Patroclus comes to Achilles in a dream for exactly this, and Elpenor waylays Odysseus about it in the underworld.

Erebus, primordial Darkness, fathered Charon upon Nyx.

Darkness and Night between them produce the ferryman, the gloom of the crossing personified as the man who runs it. His parents are the conditions of the journey rather than characters in it.

Clymene, an Oceanid, is a daughter of Oceanus and Tethys.

The three thousand Oceanids are the springs, rivers and rainclouds distributed across the world, and Hesiod says no one can name them all — only those who live nearby know each one's name.

Tethys bore the three thousand Oceanids, Clymene among them.

Clymene is the Oceanid the myths use most, as mother of the Iapetids and, in Ovid, of Phaethon by Helios. She is the point where the water-nymphs connect to the two families that trouble Zeus.

Epimetheus, the afterthinker, is a son of Iapetus and Clymene.

Prometheus warned him to accept nothing from Zeus, and he accepted Pandora anyway. She opened the jar, and everything in it went out among men except hope, which stayed under the rim.
Apollo and Artemis are twins, born to Leto on Delos — he the archer of light, she of the moonlit hunt.
Zeus and Poseidon, brothers and sons of Cronus, drew lots for the world — Zeus the sky, Poseidon the sea.
Zeus and Hades, brothers, divided the cosmos — the bright heavens to one, the shadowed underworld to the other.
Poseidon and Hades, brothers who took the sea and the underworld when the sons of Cronus divided their father's realm.

Peleus and Telamon, sons of Aeacus, sailed with the Argonauts and fathered Achilles and Ajax.

The brothers killed their half-brother Phocus and were exiled separately for it, one to Phthia and one to Salamis. Their sons Achilles and Ajax were the two best fighters in the Greek army and cousins who never quarrelled.
Europa and Cadmus, children of Agenor — when Zeus carried Europa off, Cadmus was sent to find her and never returned.
Atlas and Prometheus, sons of Iapetus — one condemned to hold up the sky, the other chained for stealing fire.

Atlas and Epimetheus, brothers among the sons of Iapetus.

Atlas holds the sky up and Epimetheus lets the jar be opened: the strongest and the stupidest of the four brothers, punished in ways that fit exactly what each of them is.

When Eurydice died of a viper's bite, Orpheus — whose music could move stones and halt rivers — went down alive into the underworld to win her back. His song so charmed Hades and Persephone that they granted her release, on a single condition: he must walk ahead into the light and not look back until both had left the dark. Within a step of the surface, seized by doubt, he turned to be sure she followed — and saw her drawn back into the shadows, lost to him a second time, and now forever.

Jason could never have won the Golden Fleece without Medea, the sorceress-princess of Colchis who fell in love with him and betrayed her own father to help him — charming the sleepless dragon, and even killing her brother to cover their escape. He swore undying loyalty and carried her home to Greece, then years later cast her aside to marry a king's daughter. Medea's revenge was without mercy: a poisoned robe that burned the new bride alive, and the murder of her own children by Jason, to leave him with nothing at all.

The sculptor Pygmalion, disdainful of the women of his city, carved from ivory a statue of a woman so perfect that he fell in love with his own creation. He dressed it, spoke to it, brought it gifts, and prayed to Aphrodite for a wife as lovely as his ivory maid. The goddess granted more than he asked: when he kissed the cold lips on coming home, they warmed under his, the ivory softened into flesh, and Galatea opened her eyes upon her maker and husband.

Sister and brother among the six, and afterwards parents: Persephone was born to Demeter by Zeus, which is what gave him the standing to promise the girl to Hades without consulting her mother.

When Demeter withheld the harvest until she was returned, it was Zeus who had to give way, the only occasion in the myths where he is compelled by another god's refusal rather than by fate.

Hestia was the first swallowed and so the last disgorged, which makes her by different reckonings both the eldest and the youngest of the six.

She asked Zeus for perpetual virginity and the first portion of every sacrifice instead of a throne, and he granted both. Her yielding of an Olympian seat is what left room for Dionysus in the later lists of twelve.

Poseidon joined Hera and Athena in the one attempted coup against Zeus, binding him with a hundred knots while he slept until Thetis fetched the hundred-handed Briareus to loose him.

They shared a grudge against Troy as well: Poseidon had built its walls for Laomedon and been cheated of the wage, and Hera had been passed over by Paris.

Hera presides over marriage and Hades made the one marriage in the family that was contracted by abduction, with Zeus's private consent and no word to the bride's mother.

Hades keeps almost entirely out of the quarrels on Olympus and Hera almost entirely within them, so the two siblings scarcely appear in a scene together.

Both are wronged by Zeus and answer in opposite registers: Hera pursues his lovers and their children for decades, while Demeter simply stops the grain and waits.

Demeter's method works. It is the difference between attacking what a husband cares for and withholding what the whole order depends on.

The goddess of marriage and the goddess who refused it, sisters and near-opposites: Hera's authority runs through the wedded household, Hestia's through the hearth at the centre of it.

Hestia has almost no narrative — no lovers, no quarrels, no children — which is precisely her character, and the reason she is so rarely depicted in the myths that consume her family.

Poseidon pursued his sister while she was searching the earth for Persephone. She turned herself into a mare and hid among a herd; he became a stallion and had her regardless.

From that came the immortal horse Arion and a daughter whose name was not spoken outside the mysteries. Demeter withdrew to a cave in her rage, and the cult title Erinys — the Fury — belonged to her afterwards in Arcadia.

Poseidon and Apollo both courted Hestia, and their rivalry over her was serious enough to threaten a quarrel among the gods.

She refused both, laid her hand on Zeus's head and swore to remain unmarried, and was given the honour of the hearth instead. It is one of the few contests in the myths settled by the woman's own decision.

The abduction sets brother against sister: Hades took Persephone with Zeus's consent and Demeter's total ignorance, and Demeter's answer was to let every seed fail.

The settlement — a third of the year below, the rest above — is a division of the girl rather than a reconciliation, and the seasons are the shape of the unresolved quarrel.

The two siblings who keep out of the story: Hestia never leaves the hearth at the centre of the house and Hades never leaves the realm beneath it.

Neither takes part in the Trojan War, neither pursues mortals, and neither has a body of myth in their own name. They are the fixed points the more restless four move around.

Between them the sisters hold the two halves of survival — the grain in the field and the fire on the hearth — and both were worshipped in the house rather than chiefly in the temple.

Neither cult depended on the great sanctuaries: an offering to Hestia opened every sacrifice, and Demeter's Eleusinian rites were open to anyone, including women and slaves.

Hephaestus caught Ares in bed with his wife Aphrodite using a net of chains too fine to see, and called the gods in to look.

Demodocus sings the story in the Odyssey as comedy: the lame smith outwitting the war-god, the assembled gods laughing, and Poseidon eventually standing surety for the fine.

In the Iliad Hebe draws the bath for Ares when he comes back from the field wounded by Diomedes, and washes and dresses him.

It is a domestic scene set inside a war poem, and one of the few glimpses of the household of Olympus behaving like a household.

Hera's children stand at the two ends of a life: Eileithyia opens the womb and Ares empties the field.

Eileithyia is the more feared of the two in practice — Hera used her to delay Heracles's birth and prolong Alcmene's labour for days, which is a power over mortals that Ares never exercises so directly.

Hebe poured the nectar for the gods, and in the first book of the Iliad Hephaestus takes the wine round the hall himself, limping, to break the quarrel between his parents by making everyone laugh.

Brother and sister hold the same office at different moments, and both use it to keep the peace in a violent household.

Eileithyia governs birth, and Hephaestus is the child Hera bore without a father — in Hesiod's version, produced alone out of anger at Zeus's producing Athena from his head.

He was thrown from Olympus for his lameness by the same mother, and returned only when he had trapped her in a golden throne of his own making and would not release her until his terms were met.

Both daughters work in Hera's own domain — Hebe as the goddess of youth, Eileithyia as the one who attends women in labour — and neither has a story apart from their mother.

Hebe was eventually married to the deified Heracles, the very man Hera and Eileithyia had between them tried to prevent from being born.

Both brothers were punished for their part in the war against the Olympians: Atlas was set to hold up the sky at the western edge of the world, and Menoetius was struck by a thunderbolt and driven down into Erebus.

Hesiod gives Menoetius no other act at all — he exists in the Theogony as an example of the arrogance that Zeus destroys.

The names divide the family: Prometheus is forethought and Menoetius is ruinous strength, and Hesiod sets one against the other deliberately.

Menoetius was destroyed at once for his outrage; Prometheus, who calculated, was punished far more elaborately and survived to be released.

Of the four sons of Iapetus, two were destroyed outright and two were left to demonstrate the consequences of thinking badly — Epimetheus by accepting Pandora after his brother's warning, Menoetius by needing no argument at all.

Their line is Hesiod's account of how mortal trouble entered the world through the miscalculations of Titans.

When Theseus carried the girl Helen off to Attica, her brothers Castor and Pollux invaded, recovered her and took Theseus's mother away as a servant in exchange.

It is the first abduction of Helen and the only one that was successfully reversed. After the twins were placed among the stars they were invoked as saviours by sailors, while their sister's second abduction was left to ten years of war.

Cassandra knew what her brother's voyage meant and said so, and was disbelieved as always; some accounts have her recognise him as the exposed infant returned when he came back to Troy for the funeral games.

She watched the war she had predicted arrive, survived the sack, and was carried off by Agamemnon to die in Mycenae.

Ismene loses both brothers on the same day, one attacking Thebes and one defending it, each by the other's hand.

Where Antigone answers by defying the burial ban, Ismene counsels obedience and lives — the sister the plays leave standing and say nothing further about.

Polynices is the brother Ismene will not risk her life to bury, though she later offers to share Antigone's punishment for having done it.

Antigone refuses her the share, telling her she cannot claim a death she did not earn, and the two sisters part without reconciling.

Neoptolemus, Achilles's son, cut down old King Priam at the altar on the night Troy fell.

Priam had come out to the altar for sanctuary. Neoptolemus killed his son Polites in front of him and then dragged the old king through the blood and cut him down at the altar itself — the sacrilege the Greeks were punished for on the voyage home.

Struck by one of Eros's arrows, Apollo burned with love for the nymph Daphne — who, pierced by a second, leaden arrow, could feel only revulsion and fled him. He pursued her across the countryside, gaining with every stride, until in despair she cried out to her father, a river-god, to save her. As Apollo's hand closed on her, bark sheathed her limbs and leaves crowned her head: she had become the laurel tree. Apollo took its evergreen leaves for his own emblem, the crown worn ever after by poets and victors.
The wise centaur Chiron schooled the young Heracles — until one of Heracles's own stray arrows gave Chiron his death.
Poseidon and Athena contested the patronage of Athens — his salt spring against her olive tree, which the people chose.
Ajax and Odysseus contended for the armour of dead Achilles; when it went to Odysseus, Ajax fell into fatal madness.

Phorcys, the old man of the sea, fathered the Gorgons upon his sister Ceto, and Stheno was the eldest of the three. The graph already gives Medusa both parents; her immortal sisters share them.

Where Medusa alone was born mortal, Stheno and Euryale took the deathlessness of the sea-gods' line.

Euryale is the second of the three Gorgon daughters of Phorcys and Ceto, and like Stheno she cannot die.

It was her far-carrying cry that Perseus heard behind him as he fled with Medusa's head, the sound of a sister who could pursue him forever and never avenge herself.

Hesiod names Typhon and Echidna as the parents of the Hydra, so the many-headed serpent of Lerna belongs to the same brood as Cerberus and the Chimera.

Its regeneration is a version of its father's excess: Typhon had a hundred serpent heads, and his daughter grew two for every one struck away.

Apollodorus makes the Sphinx a daughter of Typhon and Echidna, though Hesiod assigns her instead to Orthrus and the Chimera — one of several places where the monstrous genealogies disagree.

Either way she belongs to the same line of hybrid creatures, and she was sent against Thebes by a god rather than acting on her own account.

Apollodorus gives the Nemean Lion to Typhon and Echidna; Hesiod makes it the offspring of Orthrus and the Chimera, which would make it Echidna's grandchild rather than her son.

Its impenetrable hide is the family trait — the monsters of this line are each defined by one property no ordinary weapon can overcome.

Ladon, the hundred-headed dragon coiled about the tree of golden apples, is named a child of Typhon and Echidna by Apollodorus, though Hesiod assigns him to Phorcys and Ceto instead.

The many heads mark him as his father's son whichever version is followed.

Orthrus, the two-headed hound that guarded Geryon's red cattle, was the son of Typhon and Echidna and so the elder brother of Cerberus.

Heracles killed him in passing on the tenth labour, an obstacle rather than an opponent, though in Hesiod he goes on to father the Sphinx and the Nemean Lion upon his own mother.

When the Argo came under the Sirens' island the crew began to turn the ship toward the voices, and Orpheus took up his lyre and played louder, drowning them out until the danger was past.

It is the one recorded defeat of the Sirens by direct contest rather than by Odysseus's trick of the mast and the wax, and it turns on a singer meeting singers on their own ground.

Circe's sailing directions to Odysseus name the Sirens first among the perils ahead and prescribe the remedy exactly: wax in the crew's ears, the captain bound upright to the mast, and no man to loosen him however he pleads.

The episode works only because he is forewarned, which makes Circe — the enchantress who first detained him — the reason he survives the voyage at all.

In Apollonius, Hera and Athena cannot make Medea help Jason and so go to Aphrodite, who sends her son to do it; Eros shoots the arrow into Medea as she stands in her father's hall and the burning does the rest.

Everything that follows — the fleece, the murdered brother, the killed children — descends from that single shot, which is why the poem stages it so carefully.

Stung by Apollo's mockery of his archery, Eros shot him with a golden arrow to kindle helpless love and shot Daphne with a leaden one to breed refusal, so that the god of prophecy could not foresee or prevent his own humiliation.

Ovid uses the episode to establish that desire outranks every other divine power, including Apollo's.

Hecate alone heard Persephone cry out as the earth opened, and she came to Demeter with a torch in each hand to tell her what she had heard and to search beside her.

When the girl was restored, Hecate went with her as her attendant and forerunner, which is how a goddess of crossroads and night became fixed to the story of the returning year.

After the return from the underworld Hecate became Persephone's companion and guide, going before her at each descent and each ascent.

It is an unusual relationship among the gods: not kinship, marriage or service, but an attendance freely given because of what she witnessed.

Summoned to name the killer polluting Thebes, Tiresias refused, and only under insult said what he knew: that Oedipus was the man he sought, and blind to what he was.

The blind prophet who sees and the sighted king who does not is the play's central figure, and Oedipus ends it having taken his own sight.

The two lie within a bowshot on opposite sides of the strait, a rock and a whirlpool, so that avoiding one means passing within reach of the other.

Circe advised Odysseus to hold to Scylla's side and lose six men rather than risk the whole ship in Charybdis, and the choice between two evils has carried their names ever since.

Hector's widow was allotted to Achilles's son in the division of the Trojan captives, so the woman who had lost husband, father and brothers to Achilles was given to the man who killed her son.

Euripides makes the marriage the subject of a whole play, in which she survives by endurance rather than by rescue.

At Meleager's birth the Fates told his mother Althaea that he would live only as long as a brand then burning on the hearth. She snatched it out and hid it away.

When he killed her brothers in the quarrel over the Calydonian boar's hide, she took the brand out and put it back in the fire, and he died where he stood.

Pan pursued Echo through the woods and, refused, drove the shepherds mad so that they tore her apart, leaving only her voice scattered across the hills.

It is the harsher version of her story, older than the one in which she wastes away for Narcissus, and it explains the voice without a body the same way.

The Harpies had been sent to snatch and befoul the food of the blind seer Phineus, who could not eat, and the Argonauts found him starving.

Zetes and Calais, the winged sons of the North Wind, drove the creatures off across the sea, and Phineus repaid the crew with the sailing directions that got the Argo through the Clashing Rocks.

Fleeing Corinth after killing her children, Medea came to Athens and married the childless Aegeus on the promise of an heir.

When Theseus arrived unrecognised she knew him at once and persuaded Aegeus to hand him a cup of poison, and the king dashed it from his son's lips at the last moment on seeing the sword.

Medea offered Pelias's daughters a demonstration: she cut up an old ram, boiled it with herbs, and a lamb sprang from the cauldron.

Convinced, they cut their father up and boiled him, and she withheld the herbs. It is the only one of Jason's enemies destroyed entirely by her doing, and it cost them both the throne of Iolcus.

Every head Heracles struck from the Hydra doubled, and the labour was unwinnable until Iolaus came in with a burning brand and seared each stump as it was cut.

Eurystheus refused to count the labour on the ground that Heracles had had help, which is why the tally was raised from ten to twelve.

Sisyphus chained Thanatos so that no one on earth could die, and when he was freed and Sisyphus finally brought below, he had told his wife to leave his body unburied and talked his way back up to punish her.

He stayed for years. The stone is the answer to a man who twice cheated the underworld by argument.

Becalmed off Egypt on the way home, Menelaus was told to ambush the old sea-god at noon among his seals and hold him through every shape he took — lion, serpent, water, tree — until he answered.

Proteus gave him the wind he needed, the fate of Ajax and Agamemnon, and the news that Odysseus was alive on Calypso's island.

Driven into Lake Tritonis and unable to find the sea, the Argonauts made an offering of a bronze tripod, and Triton appeared to them and pointed out the channel.

He took the tripod, gave Euphemus a clod of Libyan earth, and towed the ship clear himself, in one of the few episodes where a sea-deity simply helps.

The old nurse had raised Odysseus and then his son, and it is to her that Telemachus entrusts his secret departure for Pylos, swearing her not to tell his mother for a dozen days.

She later recognises Odysseus by the boar-scar while washing his feet, and he stops her crying out with a hand at her throat.

Hebe had poured the nectar for the gods until Zeus carried off the Trojan boy and gave him the office, after which she was married to the newly immortal Heracles.

The replacement is recorded without comment in the sources, one immortal displacing another in the household of Olympus.

Daedalus warned his son to keep the middle course — low and the sea's damp would weigh the wings, high and the sun's heat would loosen them.

Icarus climbed anyway, the wax ran, and he fell into the water that took his name. The sun destroys him without intent, which is what makes the story a warning rather than a punishment.

The labours were not freely undertaken: the Pythia set Heracles to serve his weaker cousin for ten years in expiation for killing his own children in a madness sent by Hera, and Eurystheus devised the tasks.

He refused to count two of them — the Hydra because Iolaus helped, the Augean stables because Heracles took a fee — which is how ten labours became twelve.

Briseis was taken when Achilles sacked Lyrnessus, her husband and brothers killed in the same action, and she lived in his tent as his prize.

In the ninth book he calls her his wife in all but name and asks why the Greeks should fight over Helen if a man may not love the woman he has won; in the Iliad's terms that is an argument, not a sentiment. She mourns him alone over Patroclus's body.

The swineherd's hut is where Telemachus goes first on returning from Pylos, avoiding the harbour where the suitors' ambush is waiting.

It is in that hut that Odysseus reveals himself to his son, and Eumaeus is one of only two servants told the truth before the killing in the hall, fighting beside them when it comes.

Asked to judge a contest between Apollo's lyre and Pan's pipes, Midas alone gave the prize to Pan, and Apollo gave him the ears of an ass for having judged so badly.

Midas hid them under a cap, but his barber could not keep it in and whispered it into a hole in the ground; the reeds that grew there repeated it whenever the wind blew.
